records.content:
Frequency — a raw count of observations in a category.

Relative frequency — a category’s count divided by the total n; a proportion or percent.

Bar chart — a graph of categorical frequencies or relative frequencies as bar heights; the
y-axis must start at 0 to be read honestly.

Two-way (contingency) table — a table cross-tabulating two categorical variables.

Marginal proportion — a proportion for one variable, read from a table’s row or column total,
ignoring the other variable.

Joint proportion — the proportion of all observations in one specific cell (both variables at
once).

Conditional proportion — the proportion of one variable’s categories within a single row or
column of the other variable.

Association — two categorical variables are associated when the conditional proportions of one
change noticeably across categories of the other.

Segmented (stacked) bar chart / mosaic plot — graphs that show conditional proportions within
each category, useful for spotting association.

Misleading graph — a graph (e.g., a bar chart with a truncated y-axis, or a busy pie chart) that
distorts the visual comparison without changing the underlying numbers.

Sample space (S) — the complete list of possible outcomes of a process.

Event — a subset of the sample space; something that either happens or doesn’t on a given trial.

Probability, P(A) — a number between 0 and 1 measuring how likely event A is; interpreted
here as long-run relative frequency.

Complement (A^c) — the event “A does not happen”; P(A^c) = 1 - P(A).

Law of Large Numbers — as the number of repetitions grows, the observed relative frequency of an
event settles toward its true probability.

Durable skill: quantitative communication & critical thinking

Cross-tabulated data — sales by region, satisfaction by department, defects by shift — shows up in
almost every workplace slide deck. Knowing how to pull the right proportion out of a two-way table
(marginal vs. conditional), and knowing to distrust a bar chart whose axis doesn’t start at 0, are
skills you’ll use to build honest reports and catch misleading ones long after this course ends.

This week

OpenIntro 4th ed. — finishing §3.1 (Defining Probability) and starting §3.4 (Random Variables).

By the end of this week you can:

Apply the complement rule and the addition rule (disjoint and general) to compute event
probabilities. (Apply, §3.1)

Apply the multiplication rule for independent events and explain what independence means.
(Understand, §3.1)

Construct the probability distribution of a discrete random variable and verify it sums to 1.
(Apply, §3.4)

Compute and interpret the expected value E(X) = \sum x \cdot P(x) as a long-run average.
(Apply, §3.4)

Quiz 2 (Ch 2) is given in class this week — it covers Week 2 (summarizing numerical data).

The student government’s fall fundraiser sets up a table outside the union: a $2 raffle ticket
next to it, and the campus coffee cart’s “lucky card” promotion — draw one card from a shuffled
deck, win a free drink if it’s a heart. Both games raise the same question a smart customer should
ask before playing: what are my actual chances, and what should I expect to walk away with? Last
week you learned to read probability as long-run relative frequency and met the complement rule.
This week adds two more building-block rules — for combining probabilities with “or” and with
“and” — and introduces a new tool, the random variable, that finally lets you answer the
second question: not just “will I win?” but “what’s this worth, on average?”

hierarchy.lvl2: Combining events with “or”: the addition rule
Combining events with “or”: the addition rule

records.content:
Every probability lives on the probability scale: a number from 0 (the event never happens) to
1 (it always happens) — you’ll see this written as a decimal or a percent. Recall from last week
that the complement of an event A, written A^c, is “A does not happen,” and
P(A^c) = 1 - P(A). This week’s first new idea is combining two events with the word “or.”
The union of events A and B — written A \text{ or } B — is the event that at least one
of them happens.

If A and B can never happen on the same outcome, they’re called disjoint (or mutually
exclusive), and P(A \text{ and } B) = 0. For disjoint events, probabilities simply add:P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) \qquad \text{(disjoint events)}

If A and B can happen together, adding P(A)+P(B) double-counts the outcomes where both
occur, so the general addition rule subtracts that overlap once:P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)

Here P(A \text{ and } B) is the joint probability that both events happen at once.

Worked Example 1 — the coffee cart’s lucky-card game. The cart uses a standard, well-shuffled
52-card deck; a customer draws one card, and every card is equally likely (1/52 each). Let A =
“the card is a heart” and B = “the card is a face card” (jack, queen, or king, in any suit).
There are 13 hearts, so P(A) = 13/52 = 0.25. There are 12 face cards, so
P(B) = 12/52 \approx 0.2308.

Complement. The probability of not drawing a heart: P(A^c) = 1 - 0.25 = 0.75 (75%).

Disjoint case. “Heart or spade” — a single card can’t be both suits at once, so these events are
disjoint, and P(A \text{ and spade}) = 0:P(\text{heart or spade}) = \tfrac{13}{52} + \tfrac{13}{52} = \tfrac{26}{52} = 0.50

General case. “Heart or face card” is different — the jack, queen, and king of hearts belong to
both events, so P(A \text{ and } B) = 3/52 \approx 0.0577. Simply adding P(A)+P(B) would
count those three cards twice, so the general rule subtracts the overlap:P(A \text{ or } B) = \tfrac{13}{52} + \tfrac{12}{52} - \tfrac{3}{52} = \tfrac{22}{52} \approx 0.4231

About 42.3% of draws win at least one prize.

Independence and the multiplication rule. Two events are independent if knowing the
outcome of one tells you nothing about the other — like two different customers each drawing from
their own separately shuffled deck. For independent events, the probability both happen is the
product:P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B) \qquad \text{(independent events)}

So the probability that two independent customers both draw hearts is
0.25 \times 0.25 = 0.0625 (6.25%).

The same rule governs any two independent processes, even something as ordinary as two coin
flips. Simulating 1000 pairs of independent fair-coin flips (set.seed(1209)) landed both
heads 261 times out of 1000 — an empirical probability of 261/1000 = 0.261 — close to the
theoretical 0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25 the multiplication rule predicts; the small gap is exactly the
random noise you’d expect from only 1000 repetitions.

Figure 1. A bar chart of 1000 simulated two-coin-flip repetitions shows three bars — 0 heads,
1 head, 2 heads — at heights 243, 496, and 261 out of 1000. The middle bar (exactly one head) is
roughly twice as tall as each outer bar, matching the lopsided-in-the-middle shape the
multiplication rule predicts for two independent coins.

A random variable, usually written X, assigns a number to the outcome of a random process —
dollars won, number of heads, minutes late. A discrete random variable takes on a countable
list of specific values (a continuous random variable, coming in two weeks, can take any value
in a range). The probability distribution of X is a table listing every possible value x
alongside P(x), the probability X equals that value. Because the table lists every possibility
and no two rows overlap, a valid distribution always satisfies \sum P(x) = 1.

Worked Example 2 — the fundraiser raffle. The raffle sells n=500 tickets at $2 each. Prizes:
1 grand prize of $250, 4 prizes of $50, and 20 prizes of $10; the remaining tickets win nothing.
Let X = the dollar amount a randomly selected ticket wins:

x (dollars won)

P(x)

250

1/500 = 0.002

50

4/500 = 0.008

10

20/500 = 0.040

0

475/500 = 0.950

Total

1.000

The probabilities sum to exactly 1, confirming this is a valid distribution.

Expected value. The expected value of a discrete random variable is the probability-weighted
average of its possible values:E(X) = \sum x \cdot P(x)

Here \sum means “add up every row,” x is each possible value, and P(x) is its probability.
E(X) (also written \mu, “mu”) is the long-run average — not what any single ticket wins,
but what the average payout per ticket would settle toward if the same raffle ran over and over.
Multiplying and adding row by row:E(X) = 250(0.002) + 50(0.008) + 10(0.040) + 0(0.950) = 0.50 + 0.40 + 0.40 + 0.00 = 1.30

So E(X) = \$1.30. Since a ticket costs $2, the expected net result of playing is
1.30 - 2.00 = -\$0.70 per ticket — on average, a player loses about 70 cents per ticket, which is
exactly the money that funds the student-government fundraiser. No individual ticket ever actually
wins $1.30; the number describes the average over many, many tickets.

Figure 2. A probability-distribution bar chart for the raffle has four bars at x=0,10,50,250;
the bar at x=0 towers to a height of 0.95, while the other three bars are barely visible slivers
at 0.04, 0.008, and 0.002 — a strongly lopsided distribution where “win nothing” dominates, even
though the rare big prize is what pulls E(X) up above zero.

On your TI-83/84

Enter a distribution table the same way you’d enter a frequency list: put the x-values in L1
and their probabilities P(x) in L2. Then STAT ▸ CALC ▸ 1-Var Stats L1,L2 (typing the comma
before L2) treats the probabilities as relative weights, so the calculator’s \bar{x} on screen
is E(X), and σx is the random variable’s standard deviation (next week’s topic). For
Example 2, enter 250, 50, 10, 0 in L1 and .002, .008, .04, .95 in L2;
1-Var Stats L1,L2 returns \bar{x} = 1.3, matching the hand computation above exactly.

See it in R.suppressMessages({library(mosaic); library(BSDA)})

# Worked Example 1: probability rules on a standard 52-card deck
p_heart <- 13/52
p_face  <- 12/52
p_heart_and_face <- 3/52                                   # J, Q, K of hearts
p_heart_or_face  <- p_heart + p_face - p_heart_and_face    # general addition rule
p_heart_or_spade <- 13/52 + 13/52                          # disjoint -> simple addition
p_not_heart <- 1 - p_heart                                 # complement rule
p_heart^2                                                   # multiplication rule, independent

# empirical check of the multiplication rule: 1000 pairs of independent fair coins
set.seed(1209)
sim <- do(1000) * rflip(2)
tally(~ heads, data = sim)
mean(~ (heads == 2), data = sim)     # empirical P(both heads)

# Worked Example 2: raffle distribution table and expected value
x <- c(250, 50, 10, 0)
p <- c(1/500, 4/500, 20/500, 475/500)
sum(p)            # check the distribution sums to 1
sum(x * p)         # E(X)

Running tally(~ heads, data = sim) prints exactly the 243 / 496 / 261 counts behind Figure 1, and
sum(x * p) returns 1.3, confirming E(X) = \$1.30 from Example 2.

MATH 952 skills refresher — multiplying decimals and fractions (“of” means multiply)

Every term in an expected-value sum is a multiplication, and the word “of” is your signal to
multiply. “0.008 of the $50 prizes” literally means 0.008 \times 50. To multiply decimals by
hand: multiply the digits as whole numbers, then place the decimal point by counting total decimal
places in both factors. For 250 \times 0.002: multiply 250 \times 2 = 500, then place the
decimal 3 places from the right (since 0.002 has 3 decimal places) to get 0.500. Likewise
50 \times 0.008 = 0.400 and 10 \times 0.040 = 0.400. Once every term is a decimal, add them the
same way you’d add money — line up the decimal points: 0.500 + 0.400 + 0.400 + 0.000 = 1.300.

Using last week’s shelter data, P(\text{Large}) = 67/240 \approx 0.279. What is

rule did you use?

P(\text{2 or 5}).

If two different customers place their orders independently, what is the probability both
order a latte?

Probability scale — probability is always a number from 0 (never happens) to 1 (always
happens).

Complement (A^c) — the event “A does not happen”; P(A^c) = 1 - P(A).

Union (“or”) — the event that at least one of A or B happens.

Disjoint (mutually exclusive) events — events that cannot both happen on the same outcome,
so P(A \text{ and } B) = 0.

Addition rule (disjoint) — P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B), valid only when A and B
are disjoint.

Addition rule (general) — P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B); the
subtraction removes double-counted outcomes.

Joint probability, P(A \text{ and } B) — the probability that both A and B happen.

Independent events — knowing whether one event happened gives no information about the
other.

Multiplication rule (independent events) — P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B).

Random variable (X) — a variable that assigns a number to the outcome of a random process.

Discrete probability distribution — a table of every possible value x of a discrete random
variable with its probability P(x); a valid table always has \sum P(x) = 1.

Expected value (E(X), or \mu) — \sum x \cdot P(x); the probability-weighted average
value of X, interpreted as its long-run average over many repetitions.

Durable skill: quantitative reasoning & critical thinking

Expected value is exactly how businesses and organizers decide whether a game, promotion, or risk
is worth it — an insurer pricing a policy, a marketer running a raffle, a manager weighing a costly
gamble against a safe bet all boil the decision down to one weighted-average number. Being able to
build the distribution table and compute E(X) yourself means you can check anyone’s claim about
“expected” outcomes instead of taking their word for it.

records.content:
This week

OpenIntro 4th ed. — finishing §3.4 (stopping before §3.4.3) and starting §3.5 (Continuous
Distributions).

By the end of this week you can:

Compute the standard deviation of a discrete random variable, SD(X) = \sqrt{\sum (x-\mu)^2 P(x)}.
(Apply, §3.4.2)

Explain that for a continuous random variable, probability is the area under a density curve.
(Understand, §3.5)

Identify the key features of a Normal density curve (bell-shaped, symmetric, centered at \mu,
spread out by \sigma). (Understand, §3.5)

Explain that the total area under any density curve equals 1. (Understand, §3.5)

Last week you built your first probability distribution table and used it to find a game’s expected
winnings — the long-run average payout if you played over and over. That average is only half the
story. Two games can share the exact same average payout and still feel completely different to play:
one might pay out close to that average almost every time, while the other swings wildly between a big
loss and a rare big win. This week you’ll learn to measure that swing with the standard deviation of
a random variable. Then you’ll take the first step past distributions built from a short list of
outcomes — discrete random variables — into the kind where the outcome could be any number in a
range at all, like a person’s height or how long a coffee order takes. That’s a continuous random
variable, and it’s the introduction to the bell-shaped Normal curve you’ll spend the next several
weeks with.

records.content:
A random variable X assigns a number to every outcome of a random process. Its probability
distribution lists each possible value x next to P(x), the chance that value occurs — every
P(x) is between 0 and 1, and they all add up to 1. You already met the mean, or expected
value, of X:\mu = E(X) = \sum x \cdot P(x)

Read this as a weighted average: instead of averaging every value equally, multiply each value by
how likely it is, then add the products. \mu isn’t necessarily a value X can even take on — it’s
the distribution’s balancing point, and its most useful meaning is a long-run average: if the
random process repeated itself thousands of times, the average of all those outcomes would settle in
near \mu.

records.content:
The standard deviation of a random variable, written \sigma or SD(X), measures the typical
distance an outcome lands from \mu:\sigma = SD(X) = \sqrt{\sum (x - \mu)^2\, P(x)}

Read it left to right: find each outcome’s deviation from the mean, x-\mu (this can be
negative); square every deviation so negatives don’t cancel positives; weight each squared
deviation by its probability P(x) and add them up (this sum is the variance, \sigma^2); then
undo the squaring with a square root so \sigma comes back in the same units as X.

Worked Example 1 — a warm-up with round numbers. Before the richer example below, try the
formula on the simplest possible game: flip one fair coin. Heads (probability 0.5) pays $4; tails
(probability 0.5) pays $0. Let X be the payout.

\mu = E(X) = 2 + 0 = \$2: the long-run average payout is $2. Summing the last column gives the
variance, \sigma^2 = 2 + 2 = 4, so \sigma = \sqrt{4} = \$2. Every step is a round number here on
purpose, so you can check each one in your head before the next example makes the numbers messier.

Worked Example 2 — expected winnings on a raffle ticket. A campus club sells 200 tickets at $5
each for a fundraiser. One ticket wins a $300 grand prize, four tickets win a $25 gift card, and the
remaining 195 tickets win nothing. Let X be a ticket buyer’s net winnings — the prize won minus
the $5 cost — for a single ticket.

Summing the x\cdot P(x) column gives \mu = E(X) = -\$3.00. On average, a ticket buyer loses $3
per ticket in the long run. That is exactly why the fundraiser works: multiply that average loss by
all 200 tickets sold, and 200 \times (-\$3) = -\$600 for players collectively — which means $600
raised for the club. You can check that number directly, ticket by ticket, instead of through the
probability table:

Both routes agree: $600. Summing the last column of the first table and taking the square root gives\sigma = \sqrt{458.50} \approx \$21.41.

A single ticket’s outcome typically lands about $21.41 away from that -\$3 average — a large spread
relative to the mean. Almost every ticket loses exactly $5 (close to average), but the rare $295 win
sits far out and pulls the typical distance from the mean way up. A hypothetical raffle with the same
-\$3 mean where every ticket simply lost $3 for certain would have \sigma = 0 — no spread, because
there’d be nothing uncertain about the outcome. Here \sigma \approx \$21.41 signals real risk: most
players lose a little, a few win a lot.

hierarchy.lvl2: From discrete to continuous: density curves

records.content:
Every random variable so far — carnival-game payouts, raffle winnings — has been discrete: a short list
of possible values you can put in a table and add up. Many real quantities aren’t like that. A
person’s height, an espresso machine’s steaming time, or a commute can fall anywhere along a
continuum, with no useful way to list “every possible value” one at a time. These are continuous
random variables, and they need a different tool than a probability table: a density curve.

A density curve is a smooth curve where area, not height, equals probability. The probability that
X falls between two values a and b is the area under the curve between a and b — never read a
probability directly off the curve’s height. Two properties always hold: the curve never dips below 0,
and the total area under the entire curve equals 1 (some outcome always happens). One especially
important density-curve shape — the one you’ll use for the rest of the semester — is the Normal
curve: bell-shaped, symmetric, single-peaked, centered exactly at the mean \mu, with its spread
controlled by \sigma. A Normal curve with mean \mu and standard deviation \sigma is written
N(\mu, \sigma).

Worked Example 3 — Reading area under a density curve. Suppose adult female height (inches) is
modeled by a Normal density curve N(64.5, 2.5) — a common illustrative figure for this bell shape,
not a claim about any specific real survey. What’s the probability a randomly selected woman is
between 63 and 66 inches tall? Because X is continuous, this probability is the area under the
curve between 63 and 66, not a height read off the curve. R’s xpnorm() function computes that area
(quietly converting each boundary to a standardized distance from the mean behind the scenes — a
preview of the z-score tool coming in Week 6) and reports:P(X<63)=0.2743, \qquad P(X<66)=0.7257,

so the strip between them has area P(63<X<66)=0.4515 — about 45.1% of adult women, under this model,
fall in that six-inch window. Two things this previews: first, P(X<66) already includes everything up
through 63, so the middle strip’s area is the difference of two “less-than” areas — the same
whole-minus-the-rest logic you’ll use constantly with density curves. Second, because a single exact
height is a line with zero width, the area above any one exact value is 0, so P(X=64.5)=0 even
though P(63<X<66)>0.

On your TI-83/84

The frequency-list trick from last week extends naturally to the standard deviation: enter the
raffle’s net-winnings values in L1 (295, 20, −5) and their probabilities in L2 (.005, .02, .975),
then run STAT ▸ CALC ▸ 1-Var Stats L1,L2. The calculator reads L2 as weights, so it reports x̄ =
\mu = −3 (that’s E(X)) and σx = \sigma ≈ 21.41 (that’s SD(X)) on the same screen — no
separate formula needed. For a first look at reading area under a curve, 2ND VARS (DISTR)
▸ ShadeNorm(63, 66, 64.5, 2.5) draws the bell curve from Worked Example 3, shades the region between
63 and 66, and prints the area (0.4515) right on the graph screen — a preview of the normalcdf(
function you’ll use starting next week.

See it in R.library(mosaic)

# Worked Example 2: raffle net winnings ($5 ticket, 200 sold)
x <- c(295, 20, -5)             # net winnings (prize won - $5 cost)
p <- c(0.005, 0.020, 0.975)     # 1 grand prize, 4 gift cards, 195 no-prize / 200
sum(p)                          # check: probabilities sum to 1

mu <- sum(x * p)                # E(X)
mu

sigma <- sqrt(sum((x - mu)^2 * p))   # SD(X)
sigma

# Worked Example 3 preview: area under a density curve
xpnorm(c(63, 66), mean = 64.5, sd = 2.5, plot = FALSE)
gf_dist("norm", mean = 64.5, sd = 2.5)   # draws the N(64.5, 2.5) density curve

Running this prints mu = -3 and sigma = 21.41261 — matching the by-hand table above — and
xpnorm() prints P(X ≤ 63) = 0.2743 and P(X ≤ 66) = 0.7257, the same two areas used in Worked
Example 2. gf_dist("norm", ...) draws the N(64.5, 2.5) density curve itself, a visual check that
it’s bell-shaped and centered where you’d expect.

Figure 1. A probability histogram of the raffle’s net winnings has three bars: a very tall bar at
x=-\$5 reaching a height of 0.975, a short bar at x=\$20 with height 0.02, and a barely visible bar
at x=\$295 with height 0.005. A vertical dashed line marks the mean, \mu=-\$3, sitting just to the
right of the tall -\$5 bar — most tickets lose close to the average, while the rare $295 win sits
far out in the right tail and pulls the standard deviation up to $21.41.

Figure 2. A bell-shaped Normal density curve N(64.5, 2.5) is shaded between x=63 and x=66. The
shaded strip’s area, 0.4515, is printed in the middle of the curve; the unshaded area in both tails
together equals 1-0.4515=0.5485, and the entire shaded-plus-unshaded region under the curve sums to
exactly 1.

MATH 952 skills refresher — weighted averages, squaring, and square roots

E(X)=\sum x\cdot P(x) is a weighted average: multiply each value by its own weight (here, its
probability) before adding, instead of just adding values and dividing by how many there are. A fast
check that your probabilities are legitimate weights: they must add to exactly 1 (Worked Example 2:
0.005+0.020+0.975=1.000 ✓). For the standard deviation, do the steps in order: subtract first
(x-\mu, which can be negative — that’s fine), square second (a negative squared is always
positive, e.g. (-2)^2=4), multiply and add third, and only take the square root at the very
last step, on the calculator’s \sqrt{\ \ } key, after everything is already summed. Taking the square
root too early, or forgetting to square a negative deviation, is the most common arithmetic slip on
this formula.

Week 5 — Variability of a Random Variable; Continuous Curves

records.content:
Random variable (X) — a variable that assigns a number to every outcome of a random process.

Expected value / mean of a random variable (\mu, E(X)) — the probability-weighted average of
a random variable’s possible values, \mu=\sum x\cdot P(x); best interpreted as a long-run average
over many repetitions.

Weighted average — an average in which some values count more than others because they’re
multiplied by a weight (here, a probability) before summing.

Deviation — how far a value sits from the mean, x-\mu; can be positive or negative.

Variance (\sigma^2) — the probability-weighted average of the squared deviations,
\sum(x-\mu)^2 P(x).

Standard deviation of a random variable (\sigma, SD(X)) — the square root of the variance;
the typical distance an outcome falls from \mu, in the same units as X.

Continuous random variable — a random variable that can take any value along a continuum (no
gaps), so its possible values can’t be listed in a table.

Density curve — a smooth curve describing a continuous random variable, where area under the
curve equals probability; the curve is never negative, and the total area under it always equals
1.

Normal distribution, N(\mu,\sigma) — a specific bell-shaped, symmetric, single-peaked density
curve centered at \mu with spread controlled by \sigma.

Durable skill: quantitative reasoning & critical thinking

Every insurance premium, casino game, and investment product is priced using exactly the reasoning in
Worked Example 2: a company computes the expected value of a bet — often tilted in its own favor — and
prices around it, while a customer who only sees the possible upside is reasoning about the wrong
number. Being able to compute, and question, an expected value is a quantitative-reasoning skill that
transfers directly to reading a workplace risk assessment, a loan offer, or a benefits package.

This week in one line: you’ll meet the Normal curve, use the 68–95–99.7 rule to estimate
proportions without calculus, and learn the z-score, a single number for “how far from typical.”

Look back at last week’s density curves — the smooth outline you sketched over a histogram of adult
heights or test scores. Most of those curves shared one particular shape: a single hump, tallest in
the middle, tapering off evenly on both sides like a bell. That shape is common enough, and useful
enough, that it gets its own name and its own mathematical model — the Normal distribution.

This week you’ll learn to read that curve, use a simple rule to estimate proportions from it without
any calculus, and start measuring “how far from typical” a single value really is.

This week

OpenIntro 4th ed. — finishing §3.5 (Continuous Distributions).

By the end of this week you can:

Compute a z-score z=(x-\mu)/\sigma and interpret it as “how many SDs from the mean.” (Apply, §3.5)

Apply the 68–95–99.7 (empirical) rule to estimate proportions within 1/2/3 SDs. (Apply, §3.5)

Compare two values from different Normal distributions by standardizing. (Analyze, §3.5)

Sketch and shade a Normal curve to represent a stated probability. (Understand, §3.5)

Quiz 3 (Chapter 3) is given this week — it draws on this section together with 3.1’s probability
rules and 3.4’s expected value. Full percentile lookups (normalcdf/invNorm, xpnorm/xqnorm on
any cutoff) start in Week 8 (OpenIntro Chapter 4) — not next week, since Week 7 is the Exam 1 review
with no new content. This week builds the picture and the intuition those tools will run on.

A Normal distribution is a specific bell-shaped density curve: symmetric (the left half is a
mirror image of the right half) and unimodal (one hump, no second peak). Unlike the shelter or
coffee-shop tables from Week 3, a Normal curve isn’t built by counting categories — it’s a smooth
model for a numerical variable, and it’s completely described by just two numbers:

\mu (the Greek letter “mu”) — the mean, which sits exactly at the curve’s center and its peak.

\sigma (the Greek letter “sigma”) — the standard deviation, which controls how wide or narrow
the bell is. A small \sigma makes a tall, narrow bell (values cluster tightly around \mu); a
large \sigma makes a short, wide bell (values spread out).

Statisticians write X \sim N(\mu, \sigma) to mean “the variable X follows a Normal model with mean
\mu and standard deviation \sigma.” Every Normal curve — tall and narrow or short and wide — has
the same overall shape; only \mu and \sigma change where it’s centered and how spread out it is.

Why this particular shape keeps showing up. Heights, birth weights, measurement errors, and
standardized test scores all tend to look approximately Normal. The reason is that each of these
values is the net result of many small, independent factors adding together (genes, environment,
timing, rounding error). It turns out that whenever you add up a lot of small independent effects, the
result tends toward this exact bell shape — a fact called the Central Limit Theorem, which you’ll meet
properly in Week 9. For now, just trust the pattern: it’s why the Normal model is worth learning well.

Figure 1. A single bell-shaped curve, tallest and centered at \mu, falling away symmetrically on
both sides and never quite touching the horizontal axis. Two reference curves are sketched faintly
behind it: one taller and narrower (smaller \sigma) and one shorter and wider (larger \sigma), both
centered at the same \mu, showing that \sigma controls spread while \mu only shifts the center.

Because every Normal curve has the same shape, the proportion of values within a given number of
standard deviations of the mean is always the same, no matter what \mu and \sigma are. This fact is
the empirical rule (also called the 68–95–99.7 rule):

About 68% of values fall within 1 SD of the mean: the interval [\mu-\sigma,\ \mu+\sigma].

About 95% of values fall within 2 SD of the mean: the interval [\mu-2\sigma,\ \mu+2\sigma].

About 99.7% of values fall within 3 SD of the mean: the interval [\mu-3\sigma,\ \mu+3\sigma].

Running the exact Normal model in R (see See it in R below) confirms these are rounded numbers: the
precise areas are 68.27\%, 95.45\%, and 99.73\%. Because the curve is symmetric, whatever
percentage is left over after each interval splits evenly between the two tails — e.g., 100-95=5\%
left over at \pm 2 SD means 2.5\% in each tail (exactly: 2.28\% each, from 95.45\%).

Worked Example 1 — Cat weights. Suppose, for this example, adult indoor-cat body weight is modeled
as Normal with mean \mu = 10 lb and standard deviation \sigma = 1.5 lb (a stated model for
practice, not a fitted real dataset — the exact Normal fit for a real shelter population is a job for
later coursework). Using the empirical rule:

SDs from mean

Interval

Approx. % of cats

1

[8.5,\ 11.5] lb

68%

2

[7,\ 13] lb

95%

3

[5.5,\ 14.5] lb

99.7%

So about 68% of cats weigh between 8.5 and 11.5 lb, and only about 2.5\% weigh more than 13 lb
(2 SD above the mean) — a genuinely heavy cat by this model. A cat weighing exactly 12 lb is
(12-10)/1.5 \approx 1.33 SDs above the mean — not a round grid line, so the empirical rule alone
can’t give an exact percentage. That’s exactly the gap Week 8’s tools close: R’s xpnorm reports
the precise answer, P(X>12) \approx 9.12\%, meaning about 9 in 100 cats in this model weigh more than
12 lb.

A z-score answers one question in one number: how many standard deviations is a value from the
mean, and in which direction?z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}

Subtract the mean, then divide by the standard deviation — one subtraction, one division. A positive
z means x is above the mean; negative means below; z=0 means x is the mean exactly. A value
with z=\pm1,\pm2,\pm3 sits right on one of the empirical-rule grid lines above; any other z falls
between grid lines, which is where a tool like xpnorm is most useful. Standardizing a whole
distribution means converting every value to its z-score, which always produces the standard Normal
distribution, N(0,1) — mean 0, SD 1 — the same reference curve no matter what the original \mu
and \sigma were. That shared reference curve is exactly what lets you compare values from two
different Normal models on equal footing.

Worked Example 2 — Commute times. Suppose commute times to campus are modeled as Normal with
\mu=32 minutes and \sigma=8 minutes. A commute of 40 minutes is exactly 1 SD above the mean
(z=1), so the empirical rule says about 15.87\% of commutes are longer than 40 minutes. A commute
of 45 minutes gives z=(45-32)/8=1.625 — between the 1-SD and 2-SD grid lines. The empirical rule can
only say “somewhere between 15.87% and 2.28%”; xpnorm gives the exact figure, P(X>45)\approx5.21\%.

Worked Example 3 — Comparing across two different Normal models. Suppose (again, a stated model
for practice) ACT composite scores follow N(21,5) and SAT total scores follow N(1050,200) — the
ACT and SAT are two US college-entrance exams, each scored on its own scale. Student
A scores a 27 on the ACT; Student B scores a 1250 on the SAT. Raw scores aren’t comparable — a 27 and a
1250 live on completely different scales — but their z-scores are:z_A = \frac{27-21}{5} = 1.2 \qquad\qquad z_B = \frac{1250-1050}{200} = 1.0

Student A’s score sits 1.2 SDs above the ACT mean; Student B’s sits 1.0 SD above the SAT mean.
Because 1.2 > 1.0, Student A’s score is relatively higher — farther above typical within its own
distribution — even though 1250 is a much bigger raw number than 27. (A related question you’ll
answer precisely starting in Week 8: what raw score marks the cutoff for, say, the top 10% of
test-takers? That needs invNorm/xqnorm, run backwards from a percentage to a value — OpenIntro
Chapter 4.)

Figure 2. A shaded Normal curve for the commute-time model (\mu=32, \sigma=8): the region to the
right of x=45 minutes is filled in, visually thin compared to the whole area under the curve,
matching the computed 5.21\%.

Figure 3. Two Normal curves drawn on separate axes side by side — one for ACT scores centered at 21,
one for SAT scores centered at 1050 — each with a vertical mark at the student’s score. Student A’s
mark sits slightly farther out into its curve’s right tail (relative to that curve’s own width) than
Student B’s mark does in its curve, visually confirming z_A>z_B.

On your TI-83/84

There’s no calculator shortcut for the empirical rule itself — it’s fastest by hand: add/subtract
\sigma from \mu once, twice, or three times. For a z-score, key in ( x − μ ) ÷ σ directly on the
home screen. To see the shaded picture, preview 2ND VARS(DISTR) ▸ ShadeNorm(lower, upper, μ, σ) —
it draws the curve and fills in the requested region, though it won’t be graded until Week 8, when
you’ll pair it with normalcdf( for the exact area and invNorm( to go from a percentage back to a
cutoff value.

See it in R.library(mosaic)

# confirm the empirical rule from the exact Normal model (no simulation needed --
# this is a deterministic calculation, the same for any mu, sigma)
xpnorm(c(-3,-2,-1,1,2,3), mean = 0, sd = 1)   # standard-normal grid lines

# Worked Example 1: cat weights, mu = 10, sd = 1.5
xpnorm(12, mean = 10, sd = 1.5)     # off-grid cutoff -- prints z, picture, P(X>12)

# Worked Example 2: commute times, mu = 32, sd = 8
xpnorm(45, mean = 32, sd = 8)       # off-grid cutoff -- prints z, picture, P(X>45)

Running xpnorm(12, mean = 10, sd = 1.5) prints the standardized value z=1.333\ldots along with a
shaded picture and the two areas P(X\le12)=0.9088 and P(X>12)=0.0912 — matching 9.12\% above.
xpnorm(45, mean = 32, sd = 8) prints z=1.625 and P(X>45)=0.0521, matching 5.21\% above.

MATH 952 skills refresher — subtract, then divide, one step at a time

A z-score is two arithmetic steps done in order: first subtract (x-\mu), then divide by
\sigma. Skipping the parentheses and dividing first is the most common error. For the 12-lb cat:
12-10=2, then 2 \div 1.5 = 1.33\overline{3}. On a number line marked at \mu=10 with tick marks
every \sigma=1.5 (so ticks fall at 8.5,10,11.5,13,\ldots), 12 lands between the 11.5 and 13
ticks — visually confirming a z-score a little above 1 but below 2, before you even compute it exactly.

Using the cat-weight model from Worked Example 1 (\mu=10 lb, \sigma=1.5 lb), what weight range
holds the middle 68% of cats? What percent of cats weigh less than 8.5 lb?

Using the commute-time model (\mu=32 min, \sigma=8 min), what time range holds the middle 99.7%
of commutes? What percent of commutes are longer than 56 minutes?

Two commuting groups have separate Normal models: Group A \sim N(32,8) minutes, Group B
\sim N(25,5) minutes. A Group-A commuter takes 44 minutes; a Group-B commuter takes 34 minutes.
Compute each commuter’s z-score. Whose commute is more unusual relative to their own group, and
why does the raw time (44 vs. 34) not answer that question by itself?

Sketch a Normal curve for the cat-weight model and shade the region representing “cats weighing
between 7 and 13 pounds.” What percent does that shaded region represent, and which rule tells you?

Suppose CSUB students’ nightly sleep is modeled as Normal with \mu=7 hours, \sigma=1 hour. What
percent of students sleep less than 5 hours? Interpret your answer in one plain-language sentence.

In your own words, explain what a z-score of 0 means about a data value, and what a z-score of
-3 would tell you.

Normal distribution — a symmetric, unimodal, bell-shaped density curve, fully described by its
mean \mu and standard deviation \sigma; written N(\mu,\sigma).

Symmetric — the left half of a distribution mirrors the right half.

Unimodal — having exactly one peak (hump).

Empirical rule (68–95–99.7 rule) — for any Normal model, about 68% of values fall within 1 SD of
the mean, 95% within 2 SD, and 99.7% within 3 SD.

z-score — z=(x-\mu)/\sigma; how many standard deviations x is from the mean, and in which
direction (positive = above, negative = below).

Standardizing — converting a value (or a whole distribution) to z-scores so it can be compared on
the same scale as any other Normal distribution.

Standard Normal distribution, N(0,1) — the Normal model with mean 0 and SD 1; what any Normal
distribution becomes once standardized.

Durable skill: quantitative reasoning & quantitative communication

“How unusual is this?” is a question that comes up everywhere outside the classroom — a lab value
flagged on a medical chart, a factory part outside spec, a sales month that beats the average. The
z-score is a small, portable tool for turning that question into one honest number, and being able to
say “this is about 1.3 SDs above typical” instead of just “this seems high” is exactly the kind of
precise, defensible communication employers and clinicians rely on.

Work each one yourself first — cover the solution with your hand or a sheet of paper — then
check your steps against what’s shown. Every number below was computed in R (mosaic/BSDA,
R 4.5.2) so you can trust it to the decimal place.

Exam-style Example 1 (Ch 1) — Reading a study and its vocabulary

Part A — design. A campus wellness center wants to know whether a 10-minute guided morning
walk lowers self-reported stress. They recruit 60 student volunteers and use a random-number
generator to assign 30 of them to take the morning walk every day for two weeks and the other
30 to change nothing (control). At the end of two weeks, every volunteer rates their stress on
a continuous 0–10 scale.

Explanatory variable: whether a student walked or not — categorical, nominal (two
labels, “walk” / “no walk,” with no natural order).

Response variable: the stress rating — numerical, continuous (it can fall anywhere on
the 0–10 scale, and averaging it is meaningful).

Observational study or experiment? Experiment — the researchers themselves assigned the
treatment (who walks), rather than just observing an existing group of walkers.

Why does this design support a cause-and-effect claim? Because the 60 volunteers were
randomly assigned to the two groups, the walk and no-walk groups should be similar, on
average, in every other way (sleep habits, coursework, personality) before the study starts.
If stress ends up lower in the walking group, that difference isn’t explained by some other
systematic difference between the groups (a confounding variable) — it’s attributable to
the walk itself. An observational study (just asking students whether they already walk in
the morning) couldn’t rule out confounding this cleanly, because morning walkers might already
differ from non-walkers in ways connected to stress (schedule, motivation, fitness).

Part B — parameter vs. statistic. Separately, to practice the vocabulary: suppose (a luxury
real research never actually has) the true mean commute time for all 8,500 CSUB commuter
students happens to be known: \mu = 19.4 minutes — this is a parameter. A random sample
of n=6 students self-reports commute times, in minutes: 12, 25, 18, 31, 15, 22.suppressMessages({library(mosaic); library(BSDA)})
commute <- c(12, 25, 18, 31, 15, 22)
favstats(commute)
#>  min    Q1 median    Q3 max mean      sd n missing
#>   12 15.75     20 24.25  31 20.5 6.94982 6       0

The sample mean \bar{x} = 20.5 minutes is a statistic. Notice \bar{x} = 20.5 is close
to, but not exactly equal to, \mu = 19.4 — a gap of 1.1 minutes. That gap isn’t an error; it’s
ordinary sampling variability, the fact that a sample almost never lands exactly on the
population value. (We build precise tools for that gap starting in Week 9 — for now, just know
the vocabulary that separates a known-in-theory population number from a computed-from-data
sample number.)

Exam-style Example 2 (Ch 2, numerical) — mean, median, spread, and an outlier

Eleven classmates share how many songs are on their current music playlist:
18, 22, 19, 25, 21, 20, 23, 19, 24, 17, 52.songs <- c(18, 22, 19, 25, 21, 20, 23, 19, 24, 17, 52)
favstats(songs)
#>  min Q1 median   Q3 max     mean      sd  n missing
#>   17 19     21 23.5  52 23.63636 9.73933 11       0

Five-number summary: min = 17, Q_1 = 19, median = 21, Q_3 = 23.5, max = 52.

Center: the median (21 songs) is a better “typical” value here than the mean (23.6 songs) —
the mean is pulled upward by that one long playlist.

Spread: IQR = Q_3 - Q_1 = 23.5 - 19 = 4.5 songs.

Outlier check: the fences areQ_1 - 1.5 \cdot IQR = 19 - 1.5(4.5) = 12.25 \qquad Q_3 + 1.5 \cdot IQR = 23.5 + 1.5(4.5) = 30.25

The 52-song playlist is well above 30.25, so it’s a formally flagged outlier; every other
value falls inside the fences.

Read-back: because of that outlier, the distribution is right-skewed (a long tail toward
larger values), which is exactly why the mean (23.6) sits above the median (21) — the classic
mean-gets-pulled-toward-the-tail pattern from Week 2.

whether they’re satisfied with dining options:

                  dimnames = list(Outcome = c("Satisfied", "Not satisfied"),
                                   Plan = c("Basic", "Premium")))
prop.table(dining, margin = 2)   # P(Outcome | Plan) -- conditional on each column
#>                Plan
#> Outcome         Basic Premium
#>   Satisfied       0.6     0.8
#>   Not satisfied   0.4     0.2

Marginal: overall, 126/180 = 0.700, so 70.0% of all 180 students are satisfied,
ignoring plan tier entirely.

Joint: 54/180 = 0.300, so 30.0% of all 180 students are both on the Basic plan
and satisfied.

Conditional: among Basic-plan students, 54/90 = 0.600 (60.0% satisfied); among
Premium-plan students, 72/90 = 0.800 (80.0% satisfied).

Read-back: the conditional satisfaction rate jumps from 60.0% (Basic) to 80.0% (Premium) —
a 20-point gap — so plan tier and satisfaction appear associated. If they weren’t
associated, both conditional rates would sit close to the 70.0% marginal rate.

Exam-style Example 4 (Ch 3, probability rules) — complement, addition, multiplication

On a large campus, 62% of students drink coffee regularly (P(C) = 0.62) and 35% report
pulling at least one all-nighter this semester (P(N) = 0.35). Assume, for this problem, that
coffee-drinking and all-nighters are independent events.pC <- 0.62; pN <- 0.35
p_and <- pC * pN            # multiplication rule (independent)
p_or  <- pC + pN - p_and    # general addition rule
c(p_and = p_and, p_or = p_or, `1-pC` = 1 - pC, `1-p_or` = 1 - p_or)
#>  p_and   p_or   1-pC 1-p_or
#>  0.217  0.753  0.380  0.247

Multiplication rule (independence lets you multiply): P(C \text{ and } N) = 0.62 \times
0.35 = 0.217 — 21.7% of students both drink coffee and pulled an all-nighter.

Addition rule (general form, since the events can overlap): P(C \text{ or } N) = 0.62 +
0.35 - 0.217 = 0.753 — 75.3% of students did at least one of the two.

Complement: P(\text{not } C) = 1 - 0.62 = 0.38 (38% don’t drink coffee regularly), and
P(\text{neither } C \text{ nor } N) = 1 - 0.753 = 0.247 — 24.7% did neither.

Exam-style Example 5 (Ch 3, random variable) — expected value and SD of raffle winnings

A $5 fundraiser raffle ticket pays: $0 with probability 0.90, $10 with probability 0.08, and
$100 with probability 0.02.prize <- c(0, 10, 100)
p     <- c(0.90, 0.08, 0.02)
sum(p)                                  # check the distribution is valid
#> [1] 1
mu <- sum(prize * p)                    # E(prize)
sd_prize <- sqrt(sum((prize - mu)^2 * p))
mu
#> [1] 2.8
sd_prize
#> [1] 14.14779

net <- prize - 5                        # net winnings = prize - $5 ticket cost
sum(net * p)                            # E(net winnings)
#> [1] -2.2
sqrt(sum((net - sum(net * p))^2 * p))   # SD(net winnings)
#> [1] 14.14779

Check the distribution first: 0.90 + 0.08 + 0.02 = 1.00 — a valid probability
distribution.

Expected value: E(\text{prize}) = 0(0.90) + 10(0.08) + 100(0.02) = 0 + 0.8 + 2 = \$2.80.
Subtracting the $5 ticket cost, the expected net winnings are E(X) = 2.80 - 5 = -\$2.20
— on average, a player loses $2.20 per ticket. That’s normal for a fundraiser: the raffle is
designed to have negative expected value for the player, since the difference funds the
cause.

Standard deviation: SD(\text{prize}) = \sqrt{(0-2.8)^2(0.90) + (10-2.8)^2(0.08) +
(100-2.8)^2(0.02)} = \sqrt{200.16} \approx \$14.15. Subtracting a constant (the $5 ticket
price) shifts the mean but never changes the spread, so SD(\text{net winnings}) \approx
\$14.15 too — confirmed by the R output above. That large SD relative to the $2.20 average
loss tells you why people buy raffle tickets despite a negative expected value: the small
chance of the $100 prize creates a lot of variability around that average.

Exam-style Example 6 (Ch 3, Normal model) — z-scores and the empirical rule

Exam scores in Section A are approximately Normal with \mu = 76, \sigma = 8. A Section A
student scores 92. Exam scores in Section B (a different exam) are approximately Normal with
\mu = 70, \sigma = 5. A Section B student scores 82. Whose score is more impressive,
relative to their own section?z1 <- (92 - 76) / 8
z2 <- (82 - 70) / 5
c(z1 = z1, z2 = z2)
#>  z1  z2
#> 2.0 2.4

xpnorm(92, mean = 76, sd = 8)   # exact proportion below 92 in Section A
#> If X ~ N(76, 8), then
#>   P(X <= 92) = P(Z <= 2) = 0.9772
#>   P(X >  92) = P(Z >  2) = 0.02275

Standardize both scores: z_1 = (92-76)/8 = 2.0 and z_2 = (82-70)/5 = 2.4. Even though 92
is a higher raw score than 82, the Section B student is farther above their own class’s mean
(2.4 SDs vs. 2.0 SDs) — so the Section B score is the more impressive one, relative to its own
distribution. Raw scores from different distributions can’t be compared directly; z-scores put
them on the same scale.

Empirical rule, applied to Section A: about 95% of Section A scores fall within \mu \pm
2\sigma = 76 \pm 16, i.e., between 60 and 92. That leaves about 5% split between the two tails,
so roughly 2.5% of students scored above 92 — the Section A student is around the 97.5th
percentile. The exact Normal calculation (which you’ll compute directly starting in Week 8
with xpnorm/normalcdf) gives 97.72%, confirming the empirical rule’s estimate was a close
approximation, not a coincidence.

Figure 1. Two bell curves are drawn side by side: Section A’s curve centered at 76 with a
shaded right tail starting at 92 (2.0 SDs out), and Section B’s curve centered at 70 with a
shaded right tail starting at 82 (2.4 SDs out). Section B’s shaded tail is visibly thinner —
farther into its own curve’s tail — even though 82 is a smaller raw number than 92, illustrating
why standardizing, not the raw score, decides which result is relatively more impressive.

In Example 1’s wellness study, if the researchers had instead just surveyed students about
their existing morning habits (no random assignment), what type of study would that be, and
why would it not support a cause-and-effect conclusion? (Observational; a confounding
variable, like existing fitness level or schedule, could explain any stress difference.)

Using Example 2’s playlist data, what would the mean become if you dropped the 52-song
outlier and recomputed it on the other 10 values? Is it closer to or farther from the median
of 21? (Mean of the remaining 10 values ≈ 20.8 songs — much closer to the median of 21,
showing how strongly one point can pull the mean.)

In Example 3’s dining table, is “30.0% of all students are Basic-plan and satisfied” a
marginal, joint, or conditional proportion? (Joint.)

A campus flyer plots four majors’ average weekly study hours (Business 12.4, Nursing 14.1,
Psychology 13.0, CS 15.8) but starts the y-axis at 10 instead of 0. What’s the true ratio of
the tallest bar to the shortest (CS to Business), and roughly how many times more dramatic
does that gap look once the axis is truncated to start at 10? (True: 15.8/12.4 ≈ 1.27, about
27% higher. Truncated: apparent bars of 5.8 vs. 2.4, a ratio of about 2.42, i.e., about 142%
“higher” — roughly five times more dramatic than the real 27% difference, from the same four
numbers.)

If two events A and B are disjoint (they can never both happen), what is
P(A \text{ and } B), and how does the addition rule simplify? (P(A \text{ and } B) = 0;
addition rule becomes P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B).)

In Example 5’s raffle, would a $5 ticket with the same prizes but probabilities 0.80,
0.15, 0.05 (instead of 0.90, 0.08, 0.02) have a higher or lower expected net winnings than
-\$2.20? You don’t need to compute the exact value — reason from the fact that the $100
prize is now more likely. (Higher — moving probability toward the $100 prize raises
E(\text{prize}), which raises the net expected value, even though it’s still probably
negative.)

A z-score of z = -1.5 means what, in plain language? (The value is 1.5 standard
deviations below the mean.)

According to the empirical rule, about what percent of values in an approximately Normal
distribution fall more than 3 standard deviations from the mean, in either direction?
(About 0.3%, since 99.7% fall within 3 SDs.)

MATH 952 exam clinic

Three arithmetic habits cause most of the point loss on Exam 1 — none of them are new
statistics, just care with numbers:

Percents. Converting a count or proportion to a percent is one step: divide, then move
the decimal two places right (multiply by 100). 54/90 = 0.600 \rightarrow 60.0\% — don’t
stop at the decimal and call it a percent.

Order of operations in the SD formula. Square each deviation before you add them up,
and take the square root last — squaring after summing gives a wrong, meaningless number.

Reading the right cell of a table. Before you divide, ask “a percent (or proportion) of
what group?” A conditional proportion divides by a row or column total; a joint proportion
divides by the grand total. Mixing these two up is the single most common two-way-table
mistake.

Exam-day tips

Budget your time roughly by chapter weight: on a 75-minute exam, that’s about 15 minutes on
Ch 1 material, 19 minutes on Ch 2, and 41 minutes on Ch 3 — don’t let one tough Chapter 1
question eat time you need for the Chapter 3 section.

Read the whole question before you start writing — many points are lost by answering the
question you expected instead of the one actually asked (e.g., “conditional” vs. “marginal”).

Show every step. Partial credit exists for a correctly set up formula even if the final
arithmetic slips — a bare final number with no work shown often can’t earn partial credit.

Sketch and shade a Normal curve for every z-score / empirical-rule question, even if it’s not
required — it catches sign errors (above vs. below the mean) before you commit to an answer.

Bring your TI-83/84 with fresh batteries and your handwritten, front-and-back formula sheet.
No phones, no shared calculators once the exam starts.

If you finish early, don’t leave — revisit any question where you weren’t fully confident and
double-check your rounding and units (minutes vs. hours, percent vs. proportion).

Durable skill: self-directed learning & quantitative communication

Building your own formula sheet and working through a checklist like this one before a big
deadline is exactly the skill that transfers past this course: identifying what you actually
know versus what you’re assuming you know, then closing that gap yourself before someone else
finds it for you. Every workplace has its version of Exam 1 — a client deliverable, a budget
review, a certification exam — and the habit of honest self-assessment under a deadline is what
you’re practicing this week, not just statistics.

records.content:
This week in one line: you’ll turn any z-score into an exact probability (or work backward
from a probability to a value) using a z-table, a calculator, or R — no more “somewhere between.”

Last week you read a bell curve with the 68–95–99.7 rule, but that rule only answers questions
about whole standard deviations — “within 1 SD,” “within 2 SD.” Real questions are almost never
that tidy. A vet wants to know what fraction of adult cats weigh under a certain number of
pounds. A commuter wants to know how likely a 30-minute drive is before an 8 a.m. class. A
professor needs the exact score that separates the top 15% of an exam from everyone else — the
same kind of cutoff a clothing brand needs when it sizes a run of campus 5K t-shirts.

None of those cutoffs land on a clean whole-SD line, so this week you trade the rough guideline
for the exact tool: standardize any value into a z-score, then read off a probability (or
work backward from a probability to a value) using a z-table, a calculator, or R. Same bell
curve — just precise enough to answer any question you actually get asked.

This week

OpenIntro 4th ed. §4.1 — Working with the Normal Model.

By the end of this week you can:

Use the Normal model to find the proportion of values below, above, or between given cutoffs.
(Apply, §4.1)

Find the data value at a given percentile — the inverse Normal problem. (Apply, §4.1)

Assess whether a distribution is approximately Normal, and say when the model is a poor choice.
(Evaluate, §4.1)

Translate a real-world question (“at least,” “at most,” “the top X%”) into the correct
Normal-probability calculation. (Apply, §4.1)

records.content:
A z-score rescales a value x from a Normal model N(\mu, \sigma) into “how many standard
deviations above or below the mean” that value sits:z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}

Here x is the value you care about, \mu is the population mean, \sigma is the population
standard deviation, and z is the standardized score — negative when x is below the mean,
positive when it’s above, and unitless (pounds or minutes or points cancel out) so it always
compares to the same standard Normal model, N(0,1).

Once you have z, three equivalent tools turn it into a probability: a printed z-table
(cumulative area to the left of z), a calculator sequence, or an R function — all three read
the identical curve, so they always agree (up to rounding). A z-table is organized by row (the
ones-and-tenths digit of z) and column (the hundredths digit); the cell where they cross is
P(Z < z). Here is the row for z = -1.60 through -1.69:

z

.00

.05

To look up z = -1.67: find row -1.6, column .07, and read P(Z < -1.67) \approx 0.0475.
A table only stores z rounded to two decimals, so it’s a close approximation to the exact value
a calculator or R computes from the un-rounded z — you’ll see both below.

records.content:
Worked Example 1 — Cat weights. Model the weight of an adult indoor house cat as
X \sim N(10, 1.8) pounds. To sanity-check that shape, simulate n = 200 cats from exactly that
model (cat_weights_sim, set.seed(1209)): the sample comes back with mean 9.89 lb and median
9.85 lb — nearly identical — spread fairly evenly from a minimum of 4.53 to a maximum of
15.81 lb. A mean that close to the median, with no long stretch of extreme values on one side,
is exactly what you’d expect from a genuinely symmetric, bell-shaped population, so the Normal
model is a reasonable fit here. (It should look that way — the sample was built from a Normal
model. For real data you’d check the same two things: does the mean sit close to the median, and
does a histogram look roughly symmetric and single-peaked with no long one-sided tail? A variable
like household income, which has a long right tail of high earners, fails that check badly and
the Normal model would be a poor, misleading choice for it.)

(a) Below a cutoff. A vet flags an adult cat under 7 lb for a closer look. Standardize:
z = (7-10)/1.8 = -1.667. Here’s the bridge from that z-score to a probability: rounding to
z \approx -1.67 and reading the z-table row shown above (row -1.6, column .07) gives
P(X < 7) \approx 0.0475; R’s xpnorm (below), which uses the un-rounded z, gives the more
precise P(X < 7) = 0.0478 — about 4.8% of adult cats are predicted to fall below 7 lb. Every
other part of this example uses that same two-step bridge (round z to two decimals, look it up —
by table, calculator, or R) even when it isn’t spelled out again.

(b) Between two cutoffs. A “healthy range” is 8 to 12 lb. Standardizing both ends gives
z_8 = -1.111 and z_{12} = 1.111. Looking up z_{12}=1.11 in a z-table (or letting R’s
xpnorm compute it exactly below) gives P(X<12)=0.8667; the same lookup at z_8=-1.11 gives
P(X<8)=0.1333. Subtracting the two areas leaves just the region between them:
P(8 < X < 12) = P(X<12) - P(X<8) = 0.8667 - 0.1333 = 0.7335 — about 73.3%
of adult cats fall in the healthy range.

(c) Above a cutoff. An “overweight” flag is 13 lb or more. Since z_{13} = 1.667,
P(X \ge 13) = 1 - P(X<13) = 1 - 0.9522 = 0.0478 — about 4.8%. Notice this exactly matches
part (a): 7 and 13 lb are each 3 lb (1.667 SD) from the mean of 10, and a Normal curve is
symmetric, so its two matching tails always hold equal area.

Worked Example 2 — Commute times. Model the drive time to an 8 a.m. class as
X \sim N(22, 6) minutes (commute_times_sim, n=500, set.seed(1209); sample mean 22.34,
sd 5.87 — consistent with the model). “At least 30 minutes” means the value 30 and everything
above it, i.e. the right tail: z = (30-22)/6 = 1.333, so
P(X \ge 30) = 1 - P(X<30) = 1 - 0.9088 = 0.0912 — about 9.1% of commutes run 30 minutes or
longer. A “typical” commute, between 15 and 25 minutes, uses z_{15}=-1.167 and z_{25}=0.5:
P(15<X<25) = 0.6915 - 0.1217 = 0.5698 — about 57.0% of commutes fall in that typical window.

records.content:
Sometimes you’re given the probability and need the cutoff — the reverse of Examples 1–2.

Worked Example 3 — Exam scores. Model an exam score as X \sim N(72, 9) points
(exam_scores_sim, n=150, set.seed(1209); sample mean 70.89, sd 9.01 — consistent with the
model). The instructor wants the cutoff for a highest-honors citation given to the top 15% of
the class. “Top 15%” means the upper 15% of the curve, so it starts at the 100-15=85th
percentile: solving for the score with 85\% of the curve below it gives x = 81.33 — a score of
about 81.3 or higher places a student in the top 15%. The instructor also wants a cutoff to
flag the bottom 10% for extra support: that’s the 10th percentile directly, x = 60.47 — a
score of about 60.5 or lower falls in the bottom 10%.

On your TI-83/84

Both functions live under 2ND VARS (DISTR).

normalcdf(lower, upper, μ, σ) returns the area (probability) between two cutoffs — this
answers “below,” “above,” and “between” questions. For an open-ended tail, use -1E99 (the EE
key, then 99, gives scientific-notation “negative infinity”) as the lower bound for “at most,”
or 1E99 as the upper bound for “at least.”

Ex. 1(a): normalcdf(-1E99, 7, 10, 1.8) → 0.0478

Ex. 1(b): normalcdf(8, 12, 10, 1.8) → 0.7335

Ex. 1(c): normalcdf(13, 1E99, 10, 1.8) → 0.0478

Ex. 2: normalcdf(30, 1E99, 22, 6) → 0.0912; normalcdf(15, 25, 22, 6) → 0.5698

invNorm(area, μ, σ) goes the other direction: give it the area to the left, get back
the value. For a “top p%” cutoff, use invNorm(1 - p, μ, σ).

Ex. 3: invNorm(0.85, 72, 9) → 81.33 (top 15%); invNorm(0.10, 72, 9) → 60.47 (bottom 10%)

ShadeNorm(lower, upper, μ, σ), found under 2ND VARS ▸ DRAW, draws the curve with the
matching region shaded — use it to picture any of the calls above before you trust the number.

See it in R.library(mosaic)
set.seed(1209)

# Example 1 -- cat weights, model N(10, 1.8)
cat_weights_sim <- rnorm(200, mean = 10, sd = 1.8)
favstats(~ cat_weights_sim)

xpnorm(7, mean = 10, sd = 1.8)                                     # P(X < 7):  below
xpnorm(12, mean = 10, sd = 1.8) - xpnorm(8, mean = 10, sd = 1.8)   # P(8<X<12): between
1 - xpnorm(13, mean = 10, sd = 1.8)                                 # P(X > 13): above

# Example 2 -- commute times, model N(22, 6)
commute_times_sim <- rnorm(500, mean = 22, sd = 6)
favstats(~ commute_times_sim)

1 - xpnorm(30, mean = 22, sd = 6)                                   # P(X > 30)
xpnorm(25, mean = 22, sd = 6) - xpnorm(15, mean = 22, sd = 6)       # P(15<X<25)

# Example 3 -- exam scores, model N(72, 9)
exam_scores_sim <- rnorm(150, mean = 72, sd = 9)
favstats(~ exam_scores_sim)

xqnorm(0.85, mean = 72, sd = 9)   # top-15% cutoff (85th percentile)
xqnorm(0.10, mean = 72, sd = 9)   # bottom-10% cutoff

Running xpnorm(7, mean = 10, sd = 1.8) prints the exact 0.0478 used in Example 1(a), together
with a shaded picture of the curve; xqnorm(0.85, mean = 72, sd = 9) prints 81.33 the same way,
in reverse. Each xpnorm()/xqnorm() call draws its own labeled figure — three worth describing:

Figure 1. A bell curve for the cat-weight model N(10, 1.8) with the region below x=7 shaded
on the left tail; the shaded area covers about 4.8% of the total area under the curve.

Figure 2. A bell curve for the commute-time model N(22, 6) with the region above x=30 shaded
on the right tail; the shaded area covers about 9.1% of the total area under the curve.

Figure 3. A bell curve for the exam-score model N(72, 9) with a vertical line at x=81.33;
the shaded region to its right covers exactly 15% of the area, matching the target top-15% cutoff.

MATH 952 skills refresher — substituting carefully, and “at least” vs. “at most”

Order of operations in z=(x-\mu)/\sigma: the subtraction happens first, then you divide
the whole result by \sigma — treat the numerator as if it were in parentheses. For x=7,
\mu=10, \sigma=1.8: compute 7-10=-3 first, then divide, -3 \div 1.8 = -1.667. Dividing
before subtracting (e.g., 7 \div 1.8 first) gives a meaningless number.

“At least” vs. “at most”: “at least” means “this value or anything bigger” — the right
tail, so you either use normalcdf(value, 1E99, μ, σ) or take the complement
1 - P(X<\text{value}). “At most” means “this value or anything smaller” — the left tail, read
directly as normalcdf(-1E99, value, μ, σ), no complement needed. When in doubt, sketch the
curve and shade the side the phrase describes before you compute anything.

records.content:
z-score — z=(x-\mu)/\sigma; how many standard deviations a value sits above (positive) or
below (negative) the mean of its Normal model.

Standard Normal model, N(0,1) — the Normal curve with mean 0 and SD 1 that every z-score
is measured against.

z-table — a printed table of cumulative areas P(Z<z), organized by row (ones-and-tenths of
z) and column (hundredths of z); stores z rounded to two decimals.

normalcdf(lower, upper, μ, σ) — TI-83/84 function returning the area (probability) between
two cutoffs on a Normal curve; matches xpnorm(q, mean=, sd=) in R.

invNorm(area, μ, σ) — TI-83/84 function returning the value with a given area to its left
(the inverse-Normal/percentile problem); matches xqnorm(p, mean=, sd=) in R.

ShadeNorm(lower, upper, μ, σ) — TI-83/84 draw command that shades the requested region on
a Normal curve.

Percentile — the value below which a stated percentage of the distribution falls (e.g., the
85th percentile has 85% of values below it).

Cutoff / threshold — the specific data value marking a probability boundary (e.g., “the
score for the top 15%”).

Approximately Normal — a distribution close enough to bell-shaped and symmetric (mean near
median, no long one-sided tail) that the Normal model gives trustworthy probabilities.

Durable skill: quantitative reasoning & critical thinking

Setting a data-driven cutoff — an underweight threshold, a late-commute risk, an honors-score
line, a manufacturing tolerance, a credit-risk score — is a Normal-model calculation in almost
every field. Knowing how to translate a plain-English phrase like “at least” or “the top 15%”
into the right shaded region, and knowing when a bell curve is not the right model to trust, are
skills that transfer directly to any job that sets thresholds from data.

This week in one line: you’ll learn why two honest random samples give two different numbers
(sampling variability), and how to put a number on the typical size of that wobble (the standard
error).

Two campus newspapers, on the same afternoon, each poll 50 different students at random about a
proposed increase to the student recreation fee. Reporter A’s sample finds 52% in favor. Reporter
B’s sample finds 50% in favor. Both reporters did everything right — a genuine random sample, the
same question, the same day. So why don’t their numbers match, and which one (if either) is
“correct”?

This week starts Chapter 5, the conceptual heart of the semester. Any number you compute from a
sample — a percentage, an average — behaves a little like rolling a dice: draw a different sample
and you get a different number, purely from the luck of who happened to get picked. Once you can
say precisely how much that number typically wobbles from sample to sample, you have everything
you need for the confidence intervals and hypothesis tests that fill the rest of this course.

This week

OpenIntro 4th ed. — §5.1 (Point Estimates and Sampling Variability).

By the end of this week you can:

Distinguish a population parameter from a sample point estimate (p vs. \hat p, \mu vs.
\bar x). (Understand, §5.1)

Describe the sampling distribution of a statistic and explain why statistics vary sample to
sample. (Understand, §5.1)

Compute the standard error of a proportion and of a mean. (Apply, §5.1)

State the Central Limit Theorem in plain language and explain its role for large samples.
(Understand, §5.1)

Quiz 4 (Chapter 4) is given this week, covering last week’s Normal-model work. This week’s own
material (§5.1) is assessed on Quiz 5 in two weeks, then again on Exam 2 and the Final.

hierarchy.lvl2: From guess to typical guess: parameter vs. point estimate
From guess to typical guess: parameter vs. point estimate

records.content:
A parameter is a number that describes an entire population — every student at CSUB, every
part a factory makes, every possible flip of a coin. Parameters are usually unknown, often
unknowable directly. Two you’ll use constantly: the population proportion p (the fraction of the
population with some trait) and the population mean \mu (the average of some numerical variable
across the population).

A statistic is the matching number computed from a sample — the smaller group you actually got
to observe. The point estimate is a statistic used as your single best guess at the parameter: the
sample proportion \hat p (“p-hat”) estimates p, and the sample mean \bar x (“x-bar”)
estimates \mu.

Worked Example 1 — A campus fee referendum. To make the population visible for teaching (something
you never get in real research), suppose a population of N=20{,}000 CSUB students has a true
proportion p=0.55 supporting the fee measure — 11,000 support it, 9,000 oppose it (fee_poll_sim, a
simulated population built with set.seed(1209)). Reporter A’s random sample of n=50 students finds
\hat p = 0.52 (26 of 50 in favor). Here p=0.55 is the parameter — fixed, and in real life unknown —
while \hat p=0.52 is the point estimate: Reporter A’s one honest guess at p, built entirely from
the 50 students she happened to draw.

hierarchy.lvl2: Same recipe, different sample: the sampling distribution
Same recipe, different sample: the sampling distribution

records.content:
Reporter B follows the exact same recipe — random sample, n=50, same population — and gets
\hat p = 0.50 (25 of 50). Neither reporter made a mistake. This is sampling variability: a
statistic computed from a random sample naturally differs from one sample to the next, purely because
a different set of people was drawn. If you could repeat Reporter A’s poll thousands of times, each
repetition’s \hat p would land somewhere slightly different, and the full collection of those values
is called the sampling distribution of \hat p — the distribution of a statistic’s value across
every possible sample of a given size.

You can’t poll a real population a thousand times, but because we built the whole population for this
example, R can simulate it: draw 1,000 separate random samples of n=50 and record each one’s
\hat p.

Figure 1. A histogram of 1,000 simulated \hat p values (samples of n=50) is roughly bell-shaped
and symmetric, centered close to 0.55, and ranges from about 0.32 to 0.80. The average of all
1,000 estimates is 0.549 — almost exactly the true p=0.55 — showing that \hat p doesn’t
systematically run high or low. A statistic with that property is called unbiased.

hierarchy.lvl2: Standard error: putting a number on the wobble
Standard error: putting a number on the wobble

records.content:
The standard error (SE) is the standard deviation of a sampling distribution — the typical
distance a statistic lands from its parameter, measured in the statistic’s own units. For a sample
proportion:SE_{\hat p} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}

where p is the population proportion and n is the sample size (in practice \hat p substitutes for
the unknown p). For a sample mean:SE_{\bar x} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}

where \sigma is the population standard deviation (in practice the sample SD s substitutes for the
unknown \sigma). For the fee poll, SE_{\hat p} = \sqrt{0.55(0.45)/50} = 0.0704 — almost exactly the
standard deviation of the 1,000 simulated \hat p’s from Figure 1, which was 0.0707.

Worked Example 2 — Coffee price on campus. Build a second hypothetical population: N=20{,}000
purchase amounts (coffee_price_sim) generated from a Normal model targeting \mu=\$4.25,
\sigma=\$1.10 (the realized population lands at mean \$4.25, SD \$1.11 — indistinguishable from
the target for teaching purposes). One sample of n=30 purchases gives \bar x = \$4.07; a second
sample of n=30 gives \bar x = \$4.10 — again, two honest estimates, two different numbers.
Simulating 1,000 samples of n=30 gives a sampling distribution of \bar x centered at \$4.24 with
SD \$0.204, matching the formula: SE_{\bar x} = 1.10/\sqrt{30} = 0.201.

Now quadruple the fee-poll sample to n=200: SE_{\hat p} = \sqrt{0.55(0.45)/200} = 0.0352 — exactly
half of the n=50 value. Because n sits under a square root, multiplying the sample size by 4
divides the SE by \sqrt 4 = 2. The same shrinking pattern holds for the mean: bumping the
coffee-price sample from n=30 to n=100 shrinks the simulated spread from \$0.204 to \$0.109,
matching SE_{\bar x}=1.10/\sqrt{100}=0.11. Bigger samples give more precise — not more accurate,
more precise — point estimates, because a larger n shrinks the typical wobble around whatever
value the sample happens to be centered on.

Figure 2. A second histogram of 1,000 simulated \hat p’s, now from samples of n=200, is visibly
narrower than Figure 1’s — spread (SD) about 0.035 versus 0.071 — while still centered near 0.55.

hierarchy.lvl2: Same shape every time: the Central Limit Theorem
Same shape every time: the Central Limit Theorem

records.content:
Look back at Figure 1: the variable behind it is about as far from bell-shaped as a variable can be —
each student either supports the measure or doesn’t; a coin flip has no “shape.” Yet the sampling
distribution of \hat p came out bell-shaped anyway. That’s the Central Limit Theorem (CLT): for a
large enough sample size, the sampling distribution of a sample proportion or sample mean is
approximately Normal, centered at the true parameter, regardless of the shape of the underlying
population. “Large enough” is the condition the rest of this course is built on — Chapter 6 checks it
with a success–failure count for proportions, Chapter 7 with a sample-size/skew check for means — but
this week’s main idea is simpler: once n is reasonably large, you can trust the bell shape and
the SE formula to describe how a point estimate behaves, which is exactly what makes a confidence
interval (next week) possible.

Figure 3. Two histograms of simulated \bar x’s for the coffee-price example, n=30 and n=100,
drawn on the same horizontal scale: both are bell-shaped and centered near \$4.25, and the n=100
histogram is visibly the narrower of the two — the same square-root shrinkage seen in Figures 1–2, now
for a mean instead of a proportion.

On your TI-83/84

There’s no dedicated menu for the standard error by itself — key in the formula directly on the home
screen, one careful step at a time. For SE_{\hat p} with p=0.55, n=50:
2ND [√]( .55 × ( 1 − .55 ) ÷ 50 ) ENTER. For SE_{\bar x} with \sigma=1.10, n=30:
1.10 ÷ 2ND [√]( 30 ) ENTER. Watch your parentheses — the square root must wrap the entire fraction,
not just the denominator, or the calculator returns the wrong number (see this week’s MATH 952
refresher). Starting in Chapter 6, 1-PropZInt/1-PropZTest and TInterval/T-Test compute the SE
for you automatically — seeing the raw formula now is what makes those built-in tools make sense later
instead of feeling mysterious and unexplained.

See it in R.library(mosaic)
set.seed(1209)

# Worked Example 1: sampling distribution of p-hat, n = 50, true p = 0.55
sim_phat_50 <- do(1000) * mean(~support, data = resample(fee_poll_sim, size = 50))
favstats(~mean, data = sim_phat_50)
gf_histogram(~mean, data = sim_phat_50)

# same population, n = 200 (Figure 2)
sim_phat_200 <- do(1000) * mean(~support, data = resample(fee_poll_sim, size = 200))
favstats(~mean, data = sim_phat_200)

# Worked Example 2: sampling distribution of x-bar, n = 30 and n = 100
sim_xbar_30  <- do(1000) * mean(~price, data = resample(coffee_price_sim, size = 30))
sim_xbar_100 <- do(1000) * mean(~price, data = resample(coffee_price_sim, size = 100))
favstats(~mean, data = sim_xbar_30)
favstats(~mean, data = sim_xbar_100)

Running this exact code (set.seed(1209), mosaic 1.9.2) reproduces every number in this week’s
