MATH 952 skills refresher — order of operations under a square root

A standard error formula has three steps, always in this order: (1) do the arithmetic inside the
square root completely — multiply, then divide — (2) then take the square root, (3) done. For
SE_{\hat p} with p=0.55, n=50: first 0.55 \times 0.45 = 0.2475, then 0.2475 \div 50 = 0.00495,
then \sqrt{0.00495} \approx 0.0704. Taking the square root too early — say, of 0.45 alone, before
dividing by n — is the single most common error on this formula; always finish everything under the
radical sign first.

In Worked Example 1, p=0.55 and Reporter A’s sample gave \hat p = 0.52. Which of these two
numbers is the parameter and which is the point estimate? Explain the difference between them
in your own words.

Reporter B’s sample (same population, same n=50) gave \hat p = 0.50 — different from Reporter
A’s 0.52, even though both sampled the exact same population the exact same way. Is this
difference a sign that one reporter made a sampling mistake? Explain, using the term sampling
variability.

Compute SE_{\hat p} = \sqrt{p(1-p)/n} for the fee-poll population (p=0.55) at n=50 and again at
n=200. By what factor did n increase, and by what factor did the SE decrease? Compare each
answer to the simulated spreads reported in this week’s reading (0.0707 and 0.0349).

Compute SE_{\bar x} = \sigma/\sqrt n for the coffee-price population (\sigma=\$1.10) at n=30
and again at n=100. Compare each answer to the simulated spreads reported in this week’s reading
(\$0.204 and \$0.109).

The variable behind Figure 1 — whether a student supports the fee measure — is binary, nothing like
a bell curve. Yet the histogram of 1,000 simulated \hat p’s came out roughly bell-shaped and
centered near p=0.55. Name the principle that explains this pattern, and state it in your own
words.

A classmate says: “Since the SE for n=100 coffee-price samples (\$0.109) is smaller than the SE
for n=30 samples (\$0.204), every single sample of 100 will land closer to the true mean
(\$4.25) than every single sample of 30.” Explain what’s wrong with this claim, using the idea
that a standard error describes typical variability, not a guarantee.

Parameter — a number that describes an entire population (e.g., p, \mu); usually unknown.

Statistic — the matching number computed from a sample (e.g., \hat p, \bar x).

Point estimate — a statistic used as a single best guess at a parameter.

Sample proportion, \hat p (“p-hat”) — the point estimate of a population proportion p.

Sample mean, \bar x (“x-bar”) — the point estimate of a population mean \mu.

Sampling variability — the natural tendency of a statistic to differ from sample to sample.

Sampling distribution — the distribution of a statistic’s value across every possible sample of a
given size.

Standard error (SE) — the standard deviation of a sampling distribution; the typical distance a
statistic lands from its parameter. SE_{\hat p}=\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}; SE_{\bar x}=\sigma/\sqrt n.

Unbiased — a statistic whose sampling distribution is centered at the true parameter (it doesn’t
systematically run high or low, even though any single estimate can miss).

Central Limit Theorem (CLT) — for a large enough sample size, the sampling distribution of a
sample proportion or mean is approximately Normal, centered at the true parameter, regardless of the
underlying population’s shape.

Durable skill: quantitative reasoning & critical thinking

“Two polls, two different numbers — which one is wrong?” comes up constantly outside this classroom, in
election coverage, quality-control reports, and quarterly sales figures. Understanding that a single
sample estimate always carries some built-in wobble — and being able to name roughly how big that
wobble is — is what separates a reader who panics over routine noise from one who asks the sharper,
more useful question: is this difference bigger than sampling variability alone would explain?

This week in one line: you’ll turn a single wobbly point estimate into a confidence
interval — a whole range of plausible values, built as point estimate ± margin of error.

Last week you met the point estimate — a single number like \hat p or \bar x, built from
one sample, that almost never lands exactly on the true population parameter — and you learned to
measure how much that number bounces around from sample to sample with the standard error,
SE. A single number with no sense of “how far off could this be” is a weak thing to build a
decision on.

This week turns that wobbly point estimate into something far more honest: a confidence
interval — a whole range of plausible values for the parameter, built around the point estimate,
with a stated confidence level attached to how well the procedure itself performs in the long run.

By the end of this week you can:

Interpret a confidence interval correctly — the confidence-level idea — and avoid the “probability
the parameter is in this interval” error. (Understand, §5.2)

Explain how confidence level and sample size change the margin of error. (Analyze, §5.2)

Identify the critical value z^\star for common confidence levels (90/95/99%). (Remember, §5.2)

HW9 (this section) is assigned this week; Quiz 5 in Week 11 draws on this material together
with 5.1 and 5.3.

Every confidence interval has the same skeleton:\text{point estimate} \ \pm\ \text{margin of error (ME)}

The margin of error is how far, in either direction, the interval reaches from the point estimate.
For a large sample, ME = z^\star \cdot SE, where SE is last week’s standard error and z^\star
(read “z-star”) is a critical value: a fixed number of standard errors chosen so that the
interval-building procedure captures the true parameter a stated percentage of the time. Three
critical values come up constantly enough to know by name:

Confidence level

Critical value z^\star

90%

1.645

95%

1.960

99%

2.576

A higher confidence level needs a larger z^\star: capturing the truth more often requires
casting a wider net.

hierarchy.lvl2: A confidence interval for a proportion
A confidence interval for a proportion

records.content:
For a sample proportion \hat p (successes x out of n trials), the large-sample interval is\hat p \ \pm\ z^\star\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}

Worked Example 1 — library hours. CSUB surveys n=400 randomly selected students on extending
library hours to midnight during finals week; x=208 say yes, so \hat p = 208/400 = 0.52. The
standard error is SE=\sqrt{0.52(0.48)/400}\approx0.0250. For 95% confidence,
ME = 1.96(0.0250)\approx0.049, so0.52 \ \pm\ 0.049 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (0.471,\ 0.569)

We are 95% confident the true proportion of all CSUB students who favor extending library hours is
between 47.1% and 56.9%.

Figure 1. A number line centered at \hat p = 0.52, with a bracket extending 0.049 in each
direction to the endpoints 0.471 and 0.569; the bracket is exactly as wide on the left of the
center mark as on the right.

hierarchy.lvl2: A confidence interval for a mean
A confidence interval for a mean

records.content:
For a sample mean \bar x from a large sample, the parallel interval is\bar x \ \pm\ z^\star\dfrac{s}{\sqrt n}

using the sample standard deviation s as a stand-in for the (usually unknown) \sigma — reasonable
once n is large.

Worked Example 2 — used textbooks. The bookstore’s buy-back records for n=45 used statistics
textbooks show a mean resale price of \bar x = \$63.40 with s=\$14.75. The standard error is
SE = 14.75/\sqrt{45}\approx\$2.20. For 95% confidence, ME = 1.96(2.20)\approx\$4.31, giving63.40 \ \pm\ 4.31 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (\$59.09,\ \$67.71)

We are 95% confident the true mean resale price of a used statistics textbook this semester is between
$59.09 and $67.71.

“95% confident” describes the procedure, not this one interval. Before you collect data, there is a
95% chance that the random sample you’re about to draw will produce an interval that captures the true
parameter. Once the data are in hand and the interval is calculated — (0.471,0.569), say — the true
proportion either is or is not in that fixed range; there is no randomness left to attach a probability
to. The honest phrasing:

“We are 95% confident that the true [parameter] lies between [lower] and [upper]” — meaning: if this
sampling procedure were repeated many times, about 95% of the resulting intervals would capture the
true parameter.

Two common misinterpretations to avoid.

Not correct: “There is a 95% probability the true proportion is between 47.1% and 56.9%.” The
parameter is a fixed (if unknown) number, not a random variable — it does not have a “probability” of
falling anywhere.

Not correct: “95% of students’ true opinions fall in this interval.” The interval estimates one
population parameter (the overall proportion), not the spread of individual responses.

Figure 2. Twenty short horizontal brackets stacked vertically, each one a 95%-confidence interval
built from a different simulated sample drawn from the same population; a dashed vertical line marks
the one true (known, because simulated) parameter value. About nineteen of the twenty brackets cross
the dashed line and about one does not — illustrating that “95%” describes how often the method
succeeds across many samples, not the odds attached to any single bracket.

hierarchy.lvl2: Confidence level, sample size, and the width of the interval
Confidence level, sample size, and the width of the interval

records.content:
Two knobs control an interval’s width. Raise the confidence level and z^\star grows, widening the
interval — a more trustworthy net has to be cast wider. Raise the sample size n and SE shrinks
(it has \sqrt n in the denominator), narrowing the interval at a fixed confidence level. Using the
textbook-price example:

n

SE

95% margin of error

45

$2.20

$4.31

90

$1.55

$3.05

180

$1.10

$2.15

Quadrupling n (45 → 180) only cuts the margin of error roughly in half, because SE shrinks with
\sqrt n, not with n itself — more data buys precision, but at a diminishing rate.

MATH 952 skills refresher — building a ± interval

“52\% \pm 4.9\%” means: start at the center (52\%), then move that same distance (4.9 points)
both left and right. Lower endpoint = center - distance = 52-4.9=47.1; upper endpoint = center
+ distance =52+4.9=56.9. The two endpoints are always the same distance from the center — that is
what makes it a ± statement rather than two unrelated numbers.

A poll of n=250 registered voters finds 135 in favor of a ballot measure. Compute \hat p, then
build a 95% confidence interval (z^\star=1.96). State the margin of error.

Using the library-hours poll (\hat p=0.52, n=400), build a 90% confidence interval instead of
the 95% interval from the example. Is it narrower or wider? Why?

A random sample of n=36 campus coffee-shop receipts has \bar x = \$6.10 and s=\$2.40. Construct
a 95% confidence interval for the true mean receipt total.

Explain in your own words why quadrupling the sample size only cuts the margin of error in half,
rather than in fourth.

A student says, “There’s a 95% probability the true proportion favoring extended library hours is
between 47.1% and 56.9%.” What is wrong with this statement, and what is the correct interpretation?

Using the used-textbook example (\bar x=\$63.40, s=\$14.75, n=45), build a 99% confidence
interval. Is its margin of error larger or smaller than the 95% interval from the example? Why?

Confidence interval — a range of plausible values for a population parameter, built as point
estimate ± margin of error.

Confidence level — the long-run success rate of the interval-building procedure (e.g., 95%
means about 95% of intervals built this way, across repeated samples, capture the true parameter).

Margin of error (ME) — the distance the interval reaches in either direction from the point
estimate; ME = z^\star \cdot SE for a large sample.

Critical value z^\star — the number of standard errors needed on each side of the point estimate
to reach the stated confidence level (1.645 for 90%, 1.960 for 95%, 2.576 for 99%).

Durable skill: quantitative reasoning & critical thinking

News stories, campaign ads, and workplace reports constantly report a number with an implied “give or
take.” Knowing that “95% confident” describes a method’s long-run track record — not the odds on one
specific interval — is exactly the kind of careful, skeptical reading of a quantitative claim that
keeps you from over-trusting, or too quickly dismissing, a poll, a lab result, or a market forecast.

This week in a line: you’ll learn to test whether one specific claimed value is believable, using
a test statistic, a p-value, and a clear decide / fail-to-reject rule.

Last week you built a confidence interval — a whole range of plausible values for an unknown
population parameter. This week flips the question around. Instead of “what range of values is
plausible?” you’ll ask something sharper: “is this one specific claimed value believable, given what
my sample shows?” Your roommate insists the coin from the laundry room “seems unfair” — like it lands
heads more often than tails. You can’t interrogate a coin, so you flip it, count, and reason from the
data. Spelled out formally, that reasoning process is a hypothesis test, and it’s the backbone of
almost every “does this actually work?” claim you’ll meet after this course — in a lab report, a
business memo, or a news headline.

hierarchy.lvl2: Two competing claims: H_0 and H_A
Two competing claims: H_0 and H_A

records.content:
Every hypothesis test starts with two claims about a population parameter that can’t both be true. One
is the null hypothesis, H_0 — a skeptical, “nothing new going on” claim, always stated as an
equality. The other is the alternative hypothesis, H_A — what you suspect might be true instead,
stated with <, >, or \neq. The logic mirrors a courtroom: you assume H_0 (innocence) unless the
sample data gives strong enough evidence to abandon it.

If H_A uses \neq, the test is two-sided (evidence in either direction counts against H_0). If
H_A uses < or >, the test is one-sided (only evidence in the stated direction counts).

Coin fairness. No reason to suspect a particular direction, so this is two-sided:
H_0: p = 0.5 \qquad H_A: p \neq 0.5

Study-skills workshop. The workshop is designed to raise scores, so this is one-sided:
H_0: \mu = 70 \qquad H_A: \mu > 70

Figure 1. Two bell-shaped sampling-distribution sketches side by side. The left one, centered at
p_0=0.5, has both tails shaded past a marked point on either side (two-sided evidence). The right one,
centered at \mu_0=70, has only its right tail shaded past a marked point (one-sided evidence).

hierarchy.lvl2: The test statistic: how far from H_0, in SE units
The test statistic: how far from H_0, in SE units

records.content:
Once you assume H_0 is true, ask: how surprising is the sample statistic under that assumption? The
test statistic answers this the same way Week 6’s z-score did — by measuring distance in standard
error units, using the standard errors you built in Weeks 9–10:z = \frac{\hat p - p_0}{\mathrm{SE}_0}, \quad \mathrm{SE}_0=\sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}
\qquad\qquad
z = \frac{\bar x - \mu_0}{\mathrm{SE}_0}, \quad \mathrm{SE}_0=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}

Here \hat p and \bar x are the sample statistic actually observed; p_0 and \mu_0 are the
hypothesized values from H_0; and \mathrm{SE}_0 is the standard error computed as if H_0 were
true. A large |z| means the sample landed far from what H_0 predicted — evidence against it.

hierarchy.lvl2: The p-value: probability of data this extreme, if H_0 is true
The p-value: probability of data this extreme, if H_0 is true

records.content:
The p-value is the probability of getting a test statistic at least as extreme as the one you
observed, assuming H_0 is true. It is a conditional probability — conditioned on an assumption you
haven’t confirmed.

What a p-value is not

A p-value is not “the probability H_0 is true.” A p-value of 0.11 does not mean “there’s an 11%
chance the coin is fair.” It means: if the coin really were fair, samples this far from 50/50 would
turn up about 11% of the time from ordinary sampling variability alone.

The decision rule compares the p-value to a significance level \alpha — the risk of a wrong
rejection you agree to accept before seeing the data, usually \alpha=0.05 in this course:

Rule

Decision

Meaning

p-value <\alpha

Reject H_0

statistically significant evidence for H_A

p-value \geq\alpha

Fail to reject H_0

not enough evidence to abandon H_0

Failing to reject H_0 is not the same as proving H_0 true. It only means the sample didn’t give
strong enough evidence to abandon it — absence of evidence isn’t evidence of absence.

Worked Example 1 — Is the laundry-room coin fair? Simulating n=100 flips of a genuinely fair
coin (p_0=0.5, set.seed(1209)) gives 42 heads, so \hat p = 42/100 = 0.42. Under H_0,\mathrm{SE}_0 = \sqrt{\frac{0.5(0.5)}{100}} = 0.05 \qquad
z = \frac{0.42-0.5}{0.05} = -1.60

The sample proportion sits 1.60 SEs below the hypothesized 0.5. For a two-sided test, the p-value adds
both tails beyond |z|=1.60: p \approx 0.1096. Since 0.1096 \geq 0.05 = \alpha, we fail to reject
H_0: this sample of 100 flips does not give strong evidence the coin is unfair. (It might still be
biased — 100 flips just wasn’t enough to tell. More on that below.)

hierarchy.lvl2: One-sided tests, and the cost of being wrong
One-sided tests, and the cost of being wrong

records.content:
Worked Example 2 — Does the study-skills workshop raise scores? CSUB’s math-placement diagnostic
(a computer-adaptive exam scored on a 0–200 scale) has historically averaged \mu_0=70 points with a
known population standard deviation \sigma=12 (a stated benchmark built from many prior years, so
\sigma is treated as known here — the large-sample z story). This term, n=40 students completed a
new study-skills workshop before testing; simulating their scores (set.seed(1209), centered 4 points
above the historical mean to model a real but modest effect) gives \bar x = 75.15 and a sample spread
s=14.74. Since \sigma is treated as known, the test still uses \sigma, not s, in the standard
error (Week 14’s t-test will use s instead):\mathrm{SE}_0 = \frac{12}{\sqrt{40}} = 1.897 \qquad
z = \frac{75.15-70}{1.897} = 2.71

H_A:\mu>70 is one-sided, so the p-value is only the right tail beyond z=2.71: p\approx 0.0033.
Since 0.0033<0.05=\alpha, we reject H_0: this sample gives strong evidence the workshop group’s
average diagnostic score is higher than the historical 70.

Statistical significance vs. practical importance. The average shift (about 5 points) is
statistically clear, but the spread among individual students, s\approx14.74, is nearly three times
that shift — a large n makes small average effects easy to detect statistically, but a program director
still has to ask separately whether a 5-point average bump is worth the workshop’s cost and time
across students who vary that much individually.

Type I and Type II errors. No decision rule is ever certain, because you never actually know whether
H_0 is true. A Type I error is rejecting an H_0 that is actually true; by design, this happens
with probability exactly \alpha. In Example 2, if the workshop truly had no effect, a batch of 40
students would still produce a “significant” result about 5% of the time purely by chance — the price of
using \alpha=0.05. A Type II error is failing to reject an H_0 that is actually false. In
Example 1, if the laundry-room coin actually is slightly biased, 100 flips may simply not be enough
evidence to catch it — we’d fail to reject fairness even though it’s false. Which error costs more
depends on context: a factory that stops a good production line (Type I) wastes time and money; a
factory that lets a broken line keep running (Type II) ships defective product.

On your TI-83/84

(\neq p_0, <p_0, >p_0), then Calculate; the screen reports z, the p-value, and \hat p.
STAT ▸ TESTS ▸ 1:Z-Test… — choose Stats, enter \mu_0, \sigma, \bar x, n, the alternative,
then Calculate; the screen reports z, the p-value, and \bar x. Both menus do exactly the
computation above — they just save the arithmetic.

# Worked Example 1: coin fairness, two-sided --------------------------------
set.seed(1209)
flips <- rflip(100, prob = 0.5)          # 42 heads out of 100 this run
prop.test(x = 42, n = 100, p = 0.5, alternative = "two.sided", correct = FALSE)

# Worked Example 2: workshop diagnostic scores, one-sided --------------------
zsum.test(mean.x = 75.15, sigma.x = 12, n.x = 40, mu = 70, alternative = "greater")

prop.test prints X-squared = 2.56, p-value = 0.1096 — note \sqrt{2.56}=1.60, the same z computed
by hand. zsum.test prints z = 2.7143, p-value = 0.003321, matching Example 2 above.

MATH 952 skills refresher — comparing two decimals

Every decision this week comes down to one comparison: is the p-value less than \alpha? Line the
decimals up on the same number of places and compare digit by digit, left to right. Is 0.1096<0.05?
Pad \alpha to 0.0500: compare the tenths digit first (1 vs. 0) — 0.1096 is bigger, so no,
fail to reject. Is 0.0033<0.05? Pad to 0.0500: tenths digits tie (0=0), so compare hundredths
(0 vs. 5) — 0.0033 is smaller, so yes, reject. The symbols < and > always point at the
smaller value.

A campus dining hall claims “at least 90% of students are satisfied with the new menu.” A student
group suspects satisfaction is actually lower and surveys a random sample to test this. State H_0
and H_A in symbols, and say whether the test is one-sided or two-sided.

Explain in your own words why “fail to reject H_0” is not the same as “H_0 is true.” Use the
coin-fairness result from Worked Example 1 in your explanation.

A classmate looks at Worked Example 2’s result (z=2.71, p\approx0.0033) and says, “That means
there’s only a 0.33% chance the workshop doesn’t work.” Explain what is wrong with that statement,
and give the correct interpretation of the p-value.

Using the coin-fairness setup from Worked Example 1 (p_0=0.5, n=100, same \mathrm{SE}_0=0.05),
suppose the sample had instead come out \hat p = 0.61. Compute the z test statistic.

A researcher sets \alpha=0.05 in advance and gets a p-value of 0.04. Should they reject or fail
to reject H_0? Now suppose they had set \alpha=0.01 instead, for that same p-value — does the
decision change? What does this tell you about the role of \alpha?

In one or two sentences, describe a real (non-classroom) situation where a Type I error and a Type II
error would have different real-world costs — for example, a medical test, a spam filter, or a
quality-control check. Name which error is more costly in your example and why.

Null hypothesis, H_0 — the skeptical, “nothing new going on” claim about a parameter, always
stated as an equality; assumed true unless the data give strong evidence otherwise.

Alternative hypothesis, H_A — the claim you suspect might be true instead, stated with
<, >, or \neq.

One-sided / two-sided test — a test where H_A points in one direction (< or >) vs. either
direction (\neq).

Test statistic — a standardized measure (here, z) of how far the sample statistic is from the
value H_0 claims, in standard-error units.

p-value — the probability of a test statistic at least this extreme, assuming H_0 is true.

Significance level, \alpha — the pre-chosen risk of a wrong rejection; commonly 0.05.

Statistically significant — the decision reached when the p-value is less than \alpha.

Type I error — rejecting a true H_0; occurs with probability \alpha by design.

Type II error — failing to reject a false H_0.

Durable skill: critical thinking & quantitative communication

“Did this actually work, or did it just look that way by chance?” is a question that follows you into
almost any job — evaluating a new sales script, a software A/B test, a treatment outcome. Hypothesis
testing gives you a disciplined, honest way to answer it, and being able to say precisely “the p-value
was 0.003, so this result is unlikely to be chance alone” — instead of just “the numbers went up” — is
exactly the defensible, evidence-based communication employers and clients expect.

Coverage: Chapters 4–5 (everything from Weeks 8–11). By teaching time, roughly Ch 4 ≈

Length: your normal 75-minute class period; ~22 items total, with at most ~18%

No makeup exams. If you miss Exam 2 for any reason, the Final absorbs its weight — showing

records.content:
Tell a population parameter (\mu, p) apart from a sample point estimate (\bar x,
\hat p), and explain that every point estimate carries sampling variability — a different
sample would produce a slightly different number.

Compute the standard error of a proportion, SE_{\hat p}=\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}, and of a
mean, SE_{\bar x}=s/\sqrt{n} — the SE is the typical size of that sample-to-sample wobble.

State the Central Limit Theorem in plain language: for a large enough sample, the sampling
distribution of \bar x (or \hat p) is approximately Normal, centered at the true parameter,
with spread equal to the SE.

Build a large-sample confidence interval as point estimate \pm\, z^*\cdot SE, and interpret
it correctly — “we are 95% confident the true [parameter] is between ___ and ___” — never “there
is a 95% probability the parameter itself falls in this interval.”

Explain how confidence level and sample size each change the margin of error: higher
confidence widens the interval; a larger n narrows it. Know the three critical values by heart:
z^*=1.645 (90%), 1.96 (95%), 2.576 (99%).

Write a null hypothesis H_0 and alternative hypothesis H_a for a one- or two-sided
claim, compute a test statistic z=(\text{estimate}-\text{null value})/SE, and use the
p-value to reach a decide / fail-to-reject conclusion at a stated significance level \alpha.

Distinguish a Type I error (rejecting a true H_0) from a Type II error (failing to
reject a false H_0), and state the real-world cost of each in a given scenario.

Distinguish statistical significance (a small p-value) from practical importance (whether
the difference is actually large enough to matter in context).

Your formula sheet may hold formulas, symbol definitions, and short notes — not worked
examples. Here is the complete list for Ch 4–5.

Concept

Formula

Symbols

z-score

z = \dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}

\mu = population mean, \sigma = population SD

SE of a sample proportion

SE_{\hat p} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}

\hat p = sample proportion, n = sample size

SE of a sample mean

SE_{\bar x} = \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}

s = sample SD (\sigma/\sqrt n if \sigma is known)

Confidence interval (general)

point estimate \pm\, z^* \cdot SE

z^* = critical value for the chosen confidence level

Margin of error

ME = z^* \cdot SE

—

Test statistic (general z-form)

z = \dfrac{\text{estimate} - \text{null value}}{SE}

evaluated using the null value in SE

Decision rule

reject H_0 if p-value < \alpha; otherwise fail to reject

\alpha = significance level

Critical values z^* (memorize — short enough to skip the sheet):

Confidence level

90%

95%

99%

z^*

1.645

1.960

2.576

Symbol legend to have memorized (notation, not formulas, so it doesn’t belong on the sheet):
\mu (population mean) vs. \bar x (sample mean); p (population proportion) vs. \hat p
(sample proportion); H_0 (null hypothesis) vs. H_a (alternative hypothesis); \alpha
(significance level, chosen before you see the data); n (sample size).

Work each one yourself first — cover the solution with your hand or a sheet of paper — then check
your steps against what’s shown. Every number below was computed in R (mosaic/BSDA, R 4.5.2,
set.seed(1209)) so you can trust it to the decimal place.

Exam-style Example 1 (Ch 4) — below, and between, on a known population

A fitness app models the length of songs on its “campus workout” playlist as approximately Normal,
X \sim N(3.5, 0.6) minutes. To sanity-check that shape, a simulated sample of n=220 songs drawn
from exactly this model comes back with mean 3.45 min and median 3.45 min — nearly identical,
which is exactly what a genuinely symmetric bell-shaped population should look like.suppressMessages({library(mosaic); library(BSDA)})
set.seed(1209)
songlen_sim <- rnorm(220, mean = 3.5, sd = 0.6)
favstats(~songlen_sim)
#>       min       Q1   median       Q3      max     mean     sd   n missing
#>  1.675453 3.074937 3.453437 3.839573 5.437308 3.451742 0.6110 220       0

xpnorm(2.5, mean = 3.5, sd = 0.6)                              # P(X < 2.5): short-track flag
xpnorm(4.5, mean = 3.5, sd = 0.6) - xpnorm(3, mean = 3.5, sd = 0.6)   # P(3<X<4.5): typical window

Below a cutoff. A “short track” is flagged under 2.5 minutes: z=(2.5-3.5)/0.6=-1.667, giving
P(X<2.5)=0.0478 — about 4.8% of songs on the playlist run under 2.5 minutes.

Between two cutoffs. A “typical length” window is 3 to 4.5 minutes: z_{3}=(3-3.5)/0.6=-0.833
and z_{4.5}=(4.5-3.5)/0.6=1.667, so P(3<X<4.5)=P(X<4.5)-P(X<3)=0.7499 — about 75.0% of
songs fall in that window.

TI: normalcdf(-1E99, 2.5, 3.5, .6) → 0.0478; normalcdf(3, 4.5, 3.5, .6) → 0.7499.

Exam-style Example 2 (Ch 4) — inverse Normal on a known population

A campus fitness challenge models students’ daily step counts as X \sim N(8200, 1800) steps. A
simulated check with n=300 steps-sim values (mean 8354.5, median 8334.1, roughly symmetric
around the model’s center) is consistent with treating the model as approximately Normal. The
challenge wants two cutoffs: an “active club” badge for the top 20%, and a “check-in” flag for
the bottom 15%.steps_sim <- rnorm(300, mean = 8200, sd = 1800)
favstats(~steps_sim)
#>       min       Q1   median       Q3      max     mean      sd   n missing
#>  4276.958 7147.026 8334.075 9428.792 13231.77 8354.526 1750.336 300       0

xqnorm(0.80, mean = 8200, sd = 1800)   # top-20% cutoff = 80th percentile
xqnorm(0.15, mean = 8200, sd = 1800)   # bottom-15% cutoff = 15th percentile

Top 20% means the upper 20% of the curve, which starts at the 100-20=80th percentile:
solving gives x = 9714.9 — a student needs about 9,715 steps or more to earn the badge.

Bottom 15% is the 15th percentile directly: x = 6334.4 — about 6,334 steps or fewer
triggers the check-in flag.

TI: invNorm(.80, 8200, 1800) → 9714.9; invNorm(.15, 8200, 1800) → 6334.4.

Exam-style Example 3 (Ch 5) — point estimates, standard error, and why they wobble

Point estimates. In a sample of n=150 CSUB students, 42 report carrying a reusable water
bottle to class daily: \hat p = 42/150 = 0.28. In a separate sample of n=45 textbook prices
(dollars):water_phat <- 42/150
se_water <- sqrt(water_phat * (1 - water_phat) / 150)
c(phat = water_phat, SE = se_water)
#>  phat     SE
#>  0.28 0.0367

textbook_price <- c(78,112,95,64,130,88,101,73,119,92,84,145,67,99,108,76,
                     122,90,85,103,71,116,94,82,137,79,106,89,97,68,124,91,
                     100,86,113,74,96,128,80,105,87,118,70,102,93)
favstats(~textbook_price)
#>  min Q1 median  Q3 max     mean      sd  n missing
#>   64 82     94 108 145 96.37778 19.77865 45       0
se_book <- sd(textbook_price) / sqrt(45)
se_book
#> [1] 2.948

\hat p = 0.28 and \bar x = \$96.38 are both point estimates — single numbers computed from
one sample, standing in for the unknown population parameters p and \mu. Their standard errors
are SE_{\hat p} = \sqrt{0.28(0.72)/150} = 0.0367 and SE_{\bar x} = 19.78/\sqrt{45} = \$2.95.

Why “standard error” isn’t just jargon. Imagine (purely for demonstration — real populations
are never fully known) a hypothetical coffee-cart wait-time population that truly is
N(6, 1.5) minutes. Draw 1,000 different samples of n=40 from it and compute each sample’s mean:sim_means <- do(1000) * mean(rnorm(40, mean = 6, sd = 1.5))
favstats(~mean, data = sim_means)
#>       min       Q1   median       Q3      max     mean       sd    n missing
#>  4.93037 5.841774 5.995545 6.152879 6.743429 5.994309 0.241423 1000       0
sd(~mean, data = sim_means)          # 0.241  (simulated SD of the 1000 sample means)
1.5 / sqrt(40)                        # 0.237  (the SE formula)

The 1,000 simulated sample means center right on the true \mu=6 and spread out with SD
\approx 0.241 minutes — almost exactly the formula’s prediction, SE=1.5/\sqrt{40}=0.237. That
match is the entire point of the standard error: it is not a rounding fudge factor, it is a
genuine prediction of how far a single sample’s statistic will typically land from the truth.

Exam-style Example 4 (Ch 5) — confidence interval for a proportion

Of n=200 commuting students surveyed, 54 say they carpool at least twice a week. Build a 95%
confidence interval for the true campus-wide carpool proportion p.n <- 200; x <- 54
phat <- x / n
se <- sqrt(phat * (1 - phat) / n)
me <- 1.96 * se
c(phat = phat, SE = se, ME = me, lower = phat - me, upper = phat + me)
#>   phat     SE     ME  lower  upper
#>   0.27 0.0314 0.0615 0.2085 0.3315

\hat p = 54/200 = 0.27, SE_{\hat p} = \sqrt{0.27(0.73)/200} = 0.0314, and with z^*=1.96 for
95% confidence, ME = 1.96(0.0314) = 0.0615. The interval is
0.27 \pm 0.0615 = (0.2085,\ 0.3315).

Read-back: we are 95% confident the true proportion of all commuting students who carpool
at least twice a week is between 20.9% and 33.2%. That is not the same as “there’s a 95%
chance the true proportion is in this interval” — the true proportion is a fixed (if unknown)
number; the 95% describes how often this procedure captures it across many samples.

TI: 1-PropZInt with x=54, n=200, C-Level =.95 matches the hand calculation above exactly,
since both use the same point-estimate-±-z^*\cdot SE formula. R’s prop.test(54, 200)
reports a slightly different interval (0.211,\ 0.338) because, by default, it uses a more refined
(Wilson score, continuity-corrected) formula — close, but not identical, to the Wald formula above.
On Exam 2, use the by-hand / TI formula shown here; R is a confirmation tool, and this small
mismatch is exactly the kind of “know the technology’s limits” idea worth remembering.

Exam-style Example 5 (Ch 5) — confidence interval for a mean

A large-sample survey of n=120 first-year students finds a mean of \bar x = 6.7 hours of sleep
per night with sample SD s = 1.1 hours. Build a 90% confidence interval for the true mean sleep
\mu.xbar <- 6.7; s <- 1.1; n <- 120
se <- s / sqrt(n)
me <- 1.645 * se
c(SE = se, ME = me, lower = xbar - me, upper = xbar + me)
#>      SE     ME  lower  upper
#>  0.1004 0.1652 6.5348 6.8652

zsum.test(mean.x = 6.7, sigma.x = 1.1, n.x = 120, conf.level = 0.90)
#> 90 percent confidence interval:
#>  6.534831 6.865169

SE_{\bar x} = 1.1/\sqrt{120} = 0.1004 hours, and with z^*=1.645 for 90% confidence,
ME = 1.645(0.1004) = 0.1652 hours. The interval is 6.7 \pm 0.165 = (6.535,\ 6.865) hours, and
zsum.test confirms it exactly (means don’t have the proportion’s Wilson-vs-Wald mismatch).

Read-back: we are 90% confident the true mean nightly sleep of all first-year students is
between 6.54 and 6.87 hours — an interval that sits entirely below the commonly recommended 8
hours, worth flagging even though this exam doesn’t ask you to test that claim formally.

Exam-style Example 6 (Ch 5) — hypothesis test for a proportion

A campus tech survey claims 90% of CSUB students own a laptop (p_0 = 0.90). A random sample
of n=180 students finds 152 laptop owners. Test, at \alpha = 0.05, whether the true
proportion differs from the claim.

Step 1 — hypotheses. H_0: p = 0.90 vs. H_a: p \neq 0.90 (two-sided, since the survey claim
is simply challenged, not challenged in one direction).

Step 2 — test statistic, using the null value p_0 in the standard error:n <- 180; x <- 152; p0 <- 0.90
phat <- x / n
se0 <- sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / n)
z <- (phat - p0) / se0
p_value <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z))
c(phat = phat, SE0 = se0, z = z, p_value = p_value)
#>    phat    SE0      z p_value
#>  0.8444 0.0224 -2.485   0.013

prop.test(152, 180, p = 0.90, correct = FALSE)
#> X-squared = 6.1728, df = 1, p-value = 0.01297

\hat p = 152/180 = 0.8444, SE_0 = \sqrt{0.90(0.10)/180} = 0.0224, and
z = (0.8444-0.90)/0.0224 = -2.485, giving a two-sided p-value \approx 0.013
(prop.test’s chi-square version agrees: p=0.01297, matching since its statistic is z^2).

Step 3 — decision. Since 0.013 < \alpha = 0.05, we reject H_0: this sample gives
statistically significant evidence that the true laptop-ownership proportion differs from the
claimed 90% — specifically, the sample suggests it’s lower.

Step 4 — errors, in context. A Type I error here would be rejecting the 90% claim when it
is actually true (wrongly concluding ownership is off, when the survey’s 90% figure was correct).
A Type II error would be failing to reject the 90% claim when the true rate is actually lower
(missing a real gap in laptop access that the campus should know about) — arguably the costlier
mistake for a department planning tech-equity resources.

TI: 1-PropZTest with p_0=.90, x=152, n=180, two-sided, reports the same z and p-value.

Exam-style Example 7 (Ch 4/5 synthesis) — which tool do you reach for?

Read each scenario and decide: Normal-model probability (Ch 4), confidence interval (Ch 5), or
hypothesis test (Ch 5)? Then solve it.

Figure 1. A three-branch decision-flow diagram matching the exam’s most common setup question: what is the scenario actually asking for?

(a) “A tutoring center’s years of records show appointment lengths follow N(45, 8) minutes.
What fraction of appointments run over an hour?” Tool: Normal-model probability — \mu and
\sigma are already known population values; nothing is being estimated or tested from a sample.z = \frac{60-45}{8} = 1.875, \qquad P(X>60) = 1 - P(X<60) = 0.0304

About 3.0% of appointments run over an hour.

(b) “A campus paper wants to estimate the true percentage of all students who favor a
proposed fee change, based on a poll of 240 students in which 132 favor it.” Tool: confidence
interval — the population proportion is unknown, and the goal is to estimate it from a sample,
not test a specific claim about it.phat <- 132/240; se <- sqrt(phat*(1-phat)/240); me <- 1.96*se
c(phat = phat, lower = phat - me, upper = phat + me)
#>   phat  lower  upper
#>   0.55 0.4871 0.6129

We’re 95% confident 47.9%(lower)–61.3%(upper), more precisely (0.4871, 0.6129), of all
students favor the change — notice the interval straddles 50%, so this poll alone can’t say
whether a majority favors it.

(c) “A vending-machine company claims its machines dispense 12 oz per cup on average; a
facilities manager samples 50 cups and finds a mean of 11.7 oz with SD 0.9 oz. Are the machines
giving customers less than they paid for?” Tool: hypothesis test — there’s a specific numerical claim (\mu_0=12)
being checked against sample evidence, with a real decision (recalibrate or not) riding on it.se <- 0.9/sqrt(50); z <- (11.7-12)/se; p_value <- 2*pnorm(-abs(z))
c(SE = se, z = z, p_value = p_value)
#>     SE      z p_value
#> 0.1273 -2.357  0.0184

H_0:\mu=12 vs. H_a:\mu\neq12; z=-2.357, p-value =0.0184 < 0.05, so we reject H_0 —
statistically significant evidence the machines dispense less than the claimed 12 oz on average.

Read-back: the giveaway phrase in each scenario is the goal: “what fraction/proportion of a
known model” → probability; “estimate the true value” → confidence interval; “test a specific
claimed number” → hypothesis test. Exam 2 will often make you identify this before you can even
start computing.

Try each one on paper first. Brief answers follow so you can check yourself — no full
step-by-step solutions are given here on purpose; if your answer doesn’t match, redo the matching
worked example above before you test.

Using Example 1’s playlist model N(3.5, 0.6), what proportion of songs run over 4.5
minutes? (Same tail as the “over 60 min” idea in Example 7(a): z=1.667,
P(X>4.5)=1-0.9522=0.0478 — about 4.8%.)

In Example 2, if the challenge instead wanted the top 5% cutoff (an “elite” badge), would
that step-count value be higher or lower than the 9,715-step “top 20%” cutoff found above, and
why? (Higher — a smaller percent at the top means a farther-out, more extreme cutoff.)

In Example 3, if the water-bottle sample size had been n=600 instead of n=150 (same
\hat p=0.28), would SE_{\hat p} get bigger or smaller, and by roughly what factor?
(Smaller; n is under a square root, so quadrupling n cuts the SE in half.)

In Example 4’s carpool interval (0.2085, 0.3315), is it correct to say “there’s a 95% chance
the true carpool proportion is between 20.9% and 33.2%”? Why or why not? (No — the true
proportion is fixed; the 95% describes how often the interval-building procedure captures it
across repeated samples, not a probability about this one fixed interval.)

In Example 5, would a 99% confidence interval for mean sleep be wider or narrower than the
90% interval (6.535, 6.865) shown? (Wider — higher confidence requires a bigger margin of
error, i.e., a bigger z^*, 2.576 vs. 1.645.)

In Example 6’s laptop test, if the sample had instead found exactly 162 owners out of 180
(\hat p = 0.90, matching the claim exactly), what would the test statistic z equal, and what
decision would follow? (z=0; p-value =1; fail to reject H_0 — no evidence against the
claim.)

What is the difference between a Type I and a Type II error, in one sentence each? (Type I:
rejecting a true H_0. Type II: failing to reject a false H_0.)

In Example 7, which of the three scenarios would change from a hypothesis test to a confidence
interval if the facilities manager instead asked “what’s our best estimate of the true average
fill amount?” rather than “does it differ from the claimed 12 oz?” (Scenario (c) — same data,
different goal: estimating vs. testing a specific claim.)

MATH 952 exam clinic

Three arithmetic habits cause most of the point loss on Exam 2 — none of them are new statistics,
just care with numbers:

Formula substitution, one step at a time. In z=(x-\mu)/\sigma, SE=\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat
p)/n}, or z=(\text{estimate}-\text{null value})/SE: finish the numerator completely (including
any subtraction) before you divide or take a square root. Substituting into the wrong piece
first is the single most common formula-sheet error.

Building the ± interval. A confidence interval is always [point estimate - ME, point
estimate + ME] — compute the point estimate and the margin of error as two separate numbers
first, then build the interval as the last step. Don’t try to do it all in one line.

Comparing decimals: is the p-value less than \alpha? Line the decimals up by place value
before comparing — 0.013 < 0.05 is true even though “13” looks bigger than “5” if you compare
the digits carelessly instead of the actual decimal values.

Exam-day tips

Budget your time roughly by chapter weight: on a 75-minute exam, that’s about 22 minutes on
Ch 4 material and 53 minutes on Ch 5 — don’t let one tough Normal-model question eat time you
need for the confidence-interval and hypothesis-testing section.

Before computing anything, name the tool out loud (to yourself): probability, interval, or test?
Example 7 above is exactly the drill to practice this on.

Sketch and shade a Normal curve for every Ch 4 question, and write out H_0/H_a in symbols
for every Ch 5 test question, even when not required — both catch setup errors before you commit
to an answer.

Show every step. A correctly set up formula earns partial credit even if the final arithmetic
slips; a bare final number with no work shown often cannot.

Bring your TI-83/84 with fresh batteries and your handwritten, front-and-back formula sheet. No
phones, no shared calculators once the exam starts.

If you finish early, revisit any confidence-interval or hypothesis-test question and re-read your
own interpretation sentence — “we are X% confident that...” and “there is/is not significant
evidence that...” are exact phrasings graders look for, and it’s easy to slip into the “probability
the parameter is in the interval” error under time pressure.

Durable skill: quantitative reasoning & quantitative communication

Choosing the right tool for a question — probability, interval, or test — before you touch a
formula is quantitative reasoning: matching a method to a goal instead of pattern-matching to
whichever formula you remember best. Writing the interpretation sentence correctly — “95%
confident the true value lies between ___ and ___,” not “95% probability it’s in this interval” —
is quantitative communication: saying precisely what the number does and doesn’t claim. Both
skills show up the moment you leave this course, whether you’re reading a political poll’s margin
of error, a clinical trial’s p-value, or a vendor’s “on average” claim at work.

This week in a line: you’ll build a confidence interval and run a hypothesis test for a
single population proportion.

A shelter’s adoption newsletter says “86% of our adoptions are forever homes.” A flyer outside
the Student Union claims “90% of CSUB students commute rather than live on campus.” Both are
claims about a population proportion — the share of an entire group that has some trait —
and neither claim was checked by asking every pet owner or every student. Someone sampled a
few hundred cases and reported a percentage. The last two weeks gave you the general logic of
turning a sample statistic into a confidence interval and a hypothesis test: point estimate,
standard error, critical value or p-value, decision. This week reuses every piece of that
machinery on the single most common number in daily life — a proportion — and adds exactly one
new wrinkle: a condition that tells you when the Normal-curve shortcut is trustworthy at all.

This week

OpenIntro 4th ed. — §6.1, Inference for a Single Proportion.

By the end of this week you can:

Check the success–failure condition and independence before running inference on a
proportion. (Apply, §6.1)

Construct and interpret a confidence interval for a single population proportion. (Apply,
§6.1)

Conduct a one-proportion z-test and state the conclusion in context. (Apply, §6.1)

Explain why the test’s standard error uses the null value p_0 instead of \hat p.
(Understand, §6.1)

hierarchy.lvl2: The sample proportion and the success–failure condition
The sample proportion and the success–failure condition

records.content:
Let p (the population proportion) be the true, usually unknown, share of a population that
has some trait. You estimate it with the sample proportion,\hat p = \frac{x}{n}

where x is the number of “successes” (cases with the trait) in a random sample of size n.
“Success” is just labeling language borrowed from coin flips — it means “the outcome you’re
counting,” not “a good outcome.” \hat p is a statistic; p is the parameter it estimates,
exactly the population/sample distinction from Week 1.

Every method this week leans on one fact: when a sample is big enough, the sampling
distribution of \hat p is close to Normal, centered at p, with standard error
SE = \sqrt{p(1-p)/n} — the Week 9 idea, applied to a proportion. “Big enough” has a name, the
success–failure condition: you need at least 10 expected successes and at least 10
expected failures,n\hat p \ge 10 \qquad \text{and} \qquad n(1-\hat p) \ge 10

(using p_0 in place of \hat p for a hypothesis test — more on that below). You also need
independence: the sample was drawn randomly, and if it was drawn without replacement from
a finite population, the sample is no more than about 10% of that population. Skip the check
and the whole Normal-curve shortcut — interval or test — is not trustworthy, no matter how
clean the rest of the arithmetic looks.

hierarchy.lvl2: A confidence interval for one proportion
A confidence interval for one proportion

records.content:
A confidence interval for p takes the same shape as every interval since Week 10: point
estimate ± margin of error, where the margin of error is a critical value z^* times the
standard error:\hat p \;\pm\; z^*\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}

Note the standard error above uses \hat p, not p — the whole point of the interval is that
p is unknown, so \hat p is the best available stand-in. The familiar critical values return
unchanged: z^*=1.645 for 90% confidence, z^*=1.96 for 95%, z^*=2.576 for 99%.

Worked Example 1 — are adopted pets coming back? A local animal shelter reviews its
records for the past year: of n=250 pets adopted, x=34 were returned to the shelter within
that first year.\hat p = \frac{34}{250} = 0.136

Condition check. n\hat p = 250(0.136)=34\ge10 and n(1-\hat p)=216\ge10 — both comfortably
clear the success–failure bar. The 250 adoption records were pulled at random from the
shelter’s full adoption log and represent well under 10% of “every pet ever adopted,” so
independence is reasonable too.

Building the 95% interval.SE = \sqrt{\frac{0.136(0.864)}{250}} = 0.0217 \qquad ME = 1.96(0.0217) = 0.04250.136 \pm 0.0425 \;\longrightarrow\; (0.094,\ 0.178)

Interpretation. We are 95% confident that the true proportion of all adopted pets at this
shelter that get returned within a year is between 9.4% and 17.8%. That is a statement
about the method, not this one interval: if the shelter repeated this sampling process many
times, about 95% of the resulting intervals would capture the true return rate. It is not
correct to say “there’s a 95% probability the true rate is in this interval” — the true rate is
a fixed number; it’s the interval that varies from sample to sample.

Figure 1. A number line from 0 to 0.30 marking the point estimate \hat p=0.136 with a dot
and a horizontal bracket spanning from 0.094 to 0.178, representing the 95% confidence interval;
the bracket sits entirely below 0.20, showing the true return rate is unlikely to reach 20%.

hierarchy.lvl2: Testing a claimed proportion: the one-proportion z-test
Testing a claimed proportion: the one-proportion z-test

records.content:
A hypothesis test starts from a specific claimed value, p_0, and asks whether the sample data
give good evidence against it. Following Week 11’s logic exactly:H_0: p = p_0 \qquad\qquad H_a: p \ne p_0 \ \text{(or } < p_0 \text{ or } > p_0\text{)}

Here is the one new wrinkle: the standard error in the test statistic uses p_0, not
\hat p:z = \frac{\hat p - p_0}{SE_0} \qquad\text{where}\qquad SE_0 = \sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}

Why p_0 and not \hat p? A hypothesis test is a “what if” argument: if H_0 were true
and the population proportion really were p_0, how surprising would a sample proportion this
far from p_0 be? Answering that question means describing the sampling distribution of
\hat p under the assumption that p_0 is correct — so every piece of that distribution,
including its spread, is built from p_0. Plugging in \hat p instead would quietly assume
the very thing being tested. (This is also why the success–failure condition for a test checks
np_0\ge10 and n(1-p_0)\ge10, not n\hat p.) The confidence interval has no such “what if” —
there is no claimed value to test against — so it uses the only proportion it has, \hat p.

Once you have z, get the p-value the same way as any z-test: the area in the tail(s) of the
standard Normal curve beyond z (both tails for \ne, one tail for < or >). Compare the
p-value to \alpha and decide.

Worked Example 2 — is the 90% commuter claim right? A campus flyer claims “90% of CSUB
students commute rather than live on campus” (p_0=0.90). Student government surveys a random
sample of n=120 students; x=100 say they commute. Test the claim at \alpha=0.05.H_0: p = 0.90 \qquad H_a: p \ne 0.90

Condition check. np_0 = 120(0.90)=108\ge10 and n(1-p_0)=12\ge10 — condition holds. The
sample was drawn at random, and 120 is far less than 10% of CSUB’s enrollment.\hat p = \frac{100}{120} = 0.833 \qquad SE_0 = \sqrt{\frac{0.90(0.10)}{120}} = 0.0274z = \frac{0.833 - 0.90}{0.0274} = -2.43

The two-sided p-value is the combined area beyond z=\pm2.43 under N(0,1): p-value \approx
0.0149 (about 1.5%).

Decision. Since 0.0149 < 0.05, we reject H_0. There is statistically significant
evidence that the true proportion of CSUB students who commute is different from the claimed
90% — this sample’s 83.3% commuter rate is farther below 90% than we’d expect from sampling
variability alone if 90% were really correct.

Figure 2. A standard Normal curve with both tails beyond z=-2.43 and z=+2.43 shaded; the
two shaded slivers together represent the p-value, visibly thin compared to the whole area under
the curve, matching the computed 1.49%.

On your TI-83/84

Interval: STAT ▸ TESTS ▸ 1-PropZInt — enter x (successes), n, and C-Level, then
Calculate; the screen reports the interval, \hat p, and n. Test: STAT ▸ TESTS ▸ 1-PropZTest — enter the claimed p0, x, n, and pick the alternative (≠p0, <p0, >p0),
then Calculate; the screen reports z, the p-value, and \hat p. Both menus do exactly the
arithmetic above — no new formulas to memorize, just the right numbers in the right slots.

See it in R.suppressMessages({library(mosaic); library(BSDA)})

# Worked Example 1: 95% CI for the return-rate proportion
prop.test(34, 250, conf.level = 0.95)

# Worked Example 2: two-sided test of H0: p = 0.90
prop.test(100, 120, p = 0.90, alternative = "two.sided")

Running prop.test(34, 250, conf.level = 0.95) reports \hat p = 0.136 and a 95% interval of
(0.0973,\ 0.1863) — close to, but not identical to, the by-hand (0.094,\ 0.178) above.
prop.test(100, 120, p = 0.90, alternative = "two.sided") reports z^2 (as a chi-squared
statistic) and p-value =0.0225 — close to, but not identical to, the by-hand 0.0149.

Why the small gap? By default, R’s prop.test() applies a continuity correction. It also
computes a slightly different interval formula, called a “Wilson score” interval, instead of the
\hat p\pm z^*SE formula this course teaches by hand and on the TI-84. Adding correct = FALSE
moves R’s numbers closer to the hand calculation. Either way, R agrees with the hand calculation
on what matters for a decision — reject or fail to reject, and roughly where the interval sits.
That agreement is the whole point of using R as a confirmation tool: it is outstanding at
matching careful hand work, and a poor substitute for understanding why the numbers came out
that way. Two correct methods can report slightly different decimals — recognizing that, instead
of assuming one of them must be wrong, is part of learning the limits of your tools.

MATH 952 skills refresher — count to proportion, then round sensibly

\hat p = x/n is one division: count the successes, count the sample, divide. For the shelter
example, 34\div250 on a calculator gives 0.136 exactly — no rounding needed yet. Round only
at the end, after computing SE and ME from the full-precision \hat p; rounding \hat p
early (say, to 0.14) and carrying that rounded number through the rest of the formula quietly
shifts the final interval. A quick sanity check: \hat p must always land between 0 and 1 (it’s
a proportion) — if your division gives something outside that range, you divided the wrong way
round.

A coffee shop near campus claims 80% of its customers order a drink with dairy milk. A
barista randomly pulls n=80 receipts; x=64 show a dairy-milk drink. Check the
success–failure condition and build a 90% confidence interval for the true proportion of
dairy-milk orders. Interpret it in one sentence.

A phone-battery maker claims 95% of its batteries last a full day of typical use without a
mid-day charge. A reviewer tests n=200 batteries at random; x=178 last the full day. Test
at \alpha=0.05 whether the true proportion differs from the claimed 95%. State H_0,
H_a, and check the condition before computing anything.

A food-delivery app advertises that 80% of orders arrive within 30 minutes. A student group
randomly samples n=90 delivery receipts; x=68 arrived within 30 minutes. Check the
success–failure condition and build a 95% confidence interval for the true on-time
proportion.

Suppose a separate campus survey of sleep habits reports a 95% confidence interval for the
proportion of students who get at least 7 hours of sleep on weeknights as (0.31,\ 0.58).
Write one correct sentence interpreting this interval, and name one condition that had to
hold for the interval to be trustworthy in the first place.

A streaming service claims “at least 60% of our subscribers watch primarily on a mobile
device.” A sample of n=150 subscribers finds x=79 who watch primarily on mobile. Test the
claim at \alpha=0.05 (use H_a: p<0.60). State H_0, H_a, check the condition, compute
z and the p-value, and state your conclusion in context.

In your own words, explain why the standard error in a one-proportion hypothesis test uses
the claimed value p_0, while the standard error in a one-proportion confidence interval
uses the sample value \hat p. What would go wrong if you used \hat p in the test’s
standard error instead?

Population proportion, p — the true share of an entire population that has some trait;
a parameter, usually unknown.

Sample proportion, \hat p — x/n, the share of a sample with the trait; a statistic
that estimates p.

Success–failure condition — the check n\hat p \ge 10 and n(1-\hat p)\ge10 (or
np_0\ge10, n(1-p_0)\ge10 for a test) that must hold before treating the sampling
distribution of \hat p as approximately Normal.

Null proportion, p_0 — the specific value of p claimed under H_0; used, not
\hat p, inside the test’s standard error.

One-proportion z-interval — \hat p \pm z^*\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}, a confidence
interval for a single population proportion.

One-proportion z-test — a hypothesis test of H_0: p=p_0 using
z=(\hat p-p_0)/\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}.

Durable skill: quantitative reasoning & quantitative communication

Every “X% of customers/patients/voters” headline you’ll meet after graduation is exactly this
week’s \hat p, built from some sample you never see the details of. Knowing to ask “how big
was the sample, and does it even clear the success–failure bar?” before trusting a percentage —
and being able to report a claim as “we’re 95% confident the true rate is between 9% and 18%,”
not just “about 14%” — is a portable skill for reading a market survey, a satisfaction report,
or a clinical statistic with the same honest skepticism you’re practicing here.

This week in a line: you’ll build a confidence interval and run a hypothesis test for a
single population mean, using the t-distribution.

It’s a holiday-shortened week, so campus is quieter than usual, but your two biggest new statistics
tools of the semester are due right on schedule. Last week you built a confidence interval and
ran a hypothesis test for a single proportion — a fraction of people who do something.
This week asks the parallel question about an average instead: how long does a typical nap
last between classes? Is the average commute to campus really as short as the parking office
claims? Both questions need the same two moves you already know — a confidence interval, then a
hypothesis test — but for a mean, those moves lean on a new reference distribution, because you
almost never know the population’s true spread.

hierarchy.lvl2: The t-distribution: the price of not knowing \sigma
The t-distribution: the price of not knowing \sigma

records.content:
Back in Week 9, the standard error of a sample mean was SE_{\bar x} = \sigma/\sqrt{n}, where
\sigma (population standard deviation) was simply given. In real problems, you almost never
know \sigma — all you have is your sample’s standard deviation, s. Swapping in s for
\sigma seems harmless, but it adds a second layer of guessing on top of sampling variability:
s itself bounces around from sample to sample, especially when n is small. To account for
that extra wobble, one-mean inference uses the t-distribution instead of the Normal (z)
distribution whenever \sigma is unknown — which is the normal state of affairs.

The t-distribution is bell-shaped and centered at 0, just like z, but it is flatter in the middle
and has heavier tails — more area out past \pm 2 or \pm 3 — to cover the extra
uncertainty from estimating \sigma with s. Exactly how heavy the tails are depends on the
degrees of freedom, df = n - 1: fewer degrees of freedom (smaller samples) means heavier
tails and a wider critical value; as n grows, df grows, and the t-curve tightens until it is
nearly indistinguishable from z. Running R’s qt() across a range of df makes the convergence
concrete:

df

5

10

20

30

50

100

t^* (95% CI)

2.571

2.228

2.086

2.042

2.009

1.984

For comparison, the Normal critical value is a fixed z^* = 1.960 for a 95% interval. Notice how
t^* starts well above z^* at df = 5 and steadily closes the gap — by df = 100 it is only
0.024 away from 1.960, and it would keep sliding closer as df grows further. That single row of
numbers is the large-sample story of this course: t and z agree closely once your sample is
reasonably large, but t is the honest choice whenever \sigma is estimated rather than known.

Figure 1. A t-distribution curve overlaid on a standard Normal curve, both centered at 0 and
bell-shaped, shows the t-curve sitting slightly lower at the peak and slightly higher than the
Normal curve out past \pm 2 on both sides — the “heavier tails” that make t^* larger than
z^* for the same confidence level.

hierarchy.lvl2: A confidence interval for a mean
A confidence interval for a mean

records.content:
Conditions first. Before building an interval, check: (1) independence — observations
come from a random sample or a random process, so one value doesn’t influence another; (2)
large sample or nearly normal — with n \geq 30 the Central Limit Theorem covers you even if
the data are somewhat skewed; with smaller n, the sample should show no strong skew and no
extreme outliers.

With those conditions met, the confidence interval for a population mean \mu is\bar{x} \pm t^* \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}

where \bar{x} is the sample mean, s is the sample standard deviation, n is the sample size,
s/\sqrt{n} is the standard error of the mean, and t^* is the critical value cut from
the t-distribution with df = n-1 degrees of freedom at the chosen confidence level.

Worked Example 1 — how long is a CSUB short nap?

A random sample of n = 24 students who nap between classes reported their most recent nap
length in minutes (nap_minutes_sim, a seeded simulation):20,\ 51,\ 18,\ 38,\ 35,\ 9,\ 28,\ 34,\ 10,\ 22,\ 19,\ 35,\ 10,\ 24,\ 9,\ 57,\ 21,\ 32,\ 23,\ 18,\ 32,\ 21,\ 26,\ 20

Conditions. The sample is random, so observations are reasonably independent. favstats()
gives Q_1 = 18.75 and Q_3 = 32.5, so IQR = 13.75 and the upper outlier fence is
32.5 + 1.5(13.75) = 53.125; the 57-minute nap is a mild outlier, and 51 is not. With n = 24
and only one mild outlier (no extreme skew), the near-normal condition is reasonably satisfied
for a teaching example, though a stricter analysis would flag the 57 for a closer look.

Summary statistics: \bar{x} = 25.5 minutes, s = 12.24 minutes, n = 24.

Standard error: SE_{\bar x} = s/\sqrt{n} = 12.24/\sqrt{24} = 2.50 minutes.

Critical value: df = n - 1 = 23; for 95% confidence, t^* = 2.069 (from the t-table row
for df = 23).

Margin of error: ME = t^* \cdot SE_{\bar x} = 2.069 \times 2.50 = 5.17 minutes.

Interval: 25.5 \pm 5.17 = (20.33,\ 30.67) minutes.

Interpretation: we are 95% confident that the true mean nap length among CSUB students who
nap between classes is between about 20.3 and 30.7 minutes. This is a statement about the
method’s long-run reliability, not a probability about this one interval.

Figure 2. A number line from 15 to 35 minutes marking the sample mean \bar x=25.5 with a dot and a horizontal bracket spanning from 20.33 to 30.67, representing the 95% confidence interval for the true mean nap length.

Figure 3. A histogram of the 24 nap lengths is mounded between about 10 and 35 minutes with a
thin tail stretching out to 51 and 57 minutes — a mild right skew, consistent with the mean (25.5
minutes) sitting a bit above the median (22.5 minutes) and with the single flagged outlier at 57.

hierarchy.lvl2: The one-sample t-test for a mean
The one-sample t-test for a mean

records.content:
A hypothesis test for a mean checks a claim about \mu using the same ingredients. The null
hypothesis states a specific value, H_0: \mu = \mu_0; the alternative H_a says \mu differs
from \mu_0 (two-sided) or is specifically greater than or less than it (one-sided). The test
statistic ist = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}, \qquad df = n - 1,

and the p-value is the area under the t-curve with df = n-1 degrees of freedom, out past
the observed t in the direction(s) H_a points. As always: small p-value (below your
significance level \alpha) means the data are surprising under H_0, so you reject H_0;
otherwise you fail to reject H_0.

Worked Example 2 — is the campus commute really only 20 minutes?

CSUB’s parking and transportation office advertises an average commute of 20 minutes for
commuter students. A random sample of n = 45 commuter students (commute_min_sim) reports
\bar{x} = 23.49 minutes and s = 9.39 minutes. Many students suspect the true average is
longer than advertised, so this calls for a one-sided test.

Hypotheses: H_0: \mu = 20 minutes vs. H_a: \mu > 20 minutes.

Conditions. The sample is random, and n = 45 \geq 30, so the large-sample condition covers
any mild skew in commute times.

Standard error: SE_{\bar x} = 9.39/\sqrt{45} = 1.40 minutes.

Test statistic: df = 44,t = \frac{23.49 - 20}{1.40} = 2.49.

p-value: the area under the t_{44} curve above t = 2.49 is p = 0.0083.

Decision: at \alpha = 0.05, p = 0.0083 < 0.05, so we reject H_0.

Conclusion in context: the sample gives strong evidence that the true mean commute time for
CSUB commuter students exceeds the advertised 20 minutes.

Large samples: why t and z nearly agree. Re-running Example 2’s exact summary statistics
through the z-based equivalent (same \bar x, s, and n, but referenced against the Normal
curve instead of t_{44}) gives z = 2.49 — the identical test statistic value, because the
formula is the same — with p = 0.0064, versus the t-test’s p = 0.0083. The two p-values are
close enough that both lead to the same decision at \alpha = 0.05, exactly the pattern the
t^*-vs-z^* table above predicted: once n is large (here df = 44), the extra uncertainty
from estimating \sigma with s barely matters, and t and z tell the same story. For small
samples, they can disagree more, which is why this course leads with t.

On your TI-83/84

Confidence interval — TInterval. STAT ▸ TESTS ▸ 8:TInterval. Choose Stats if you have
\bar{x}, Sx, n (Example 1: enter 25.5, 12.24, 24), or Data if the raw list is in L1.
Enter the confidence level (C-Level), then Calculate — the screen reports the interval
directly, matching (20.33, 30.67) above.

Hypothesis test — T-Test. STAT ▸ TESTS ▸ 2:T-Test. Choose Stats, enter \mu_0 (the
null value), \bar{x}, Sx, n (Example 2: \mu_0=20, 23.49, 9.39, 45), pick the alternative
(\mu_0 \neq, <, or > — here >), then Calculate. The screen reports t, df, and the
p-value, matching t = 2.49, p = 0.0083 above.

See it in R.suppressMessages({library(mosaic); library(BSDA)})

# Worked Example 1: nap length, confidence interval from raw data
nap_minutes_sim <- c(20, 51, 18, 38, 35, 9, 28, 34, 10, 22, 19, 35,
                      10, 24, 9, 57, 21, 32, 23, 18, 32, 21, 26, 20)
naps <- data.frame(nap_minutes_sim)
favstats(~ nap_minutes_sim, data = naps)
t.test(~ nap_minutes_sim, data = naps, conf.level = 0.95)$conf.int

# Worked Example 2: commute time, one-sample t-test from summary stats (BSDA)
tsum.test(mean.x = 23.49, s.x = 9.39, n.x = 45, mu = 20, alternative = "greater")

# large-sample z equivalent, same summary stats (noted, not required)
zsum.test(mean.x = 23.49, sigma.x = 9.39, n.x = 45, mu = 20, alternative = "greater")

t.test()$conf.int returns 20.33286 30.66714, matching Example 1’s hand-built interval.
tsum.test() returns t = 2.4933, df = 44, p-value = 0.008246, matching Example 2. zsum.test()
on the identical summary numbers returns z = 2.4933, p-value = 0.006329 — the same test
statistic, a slightly smaller p-value, and the same decision at \alpha = 0.05, exactly the
t-vs-z agreement described above. Use tsum.test()/zsum.test() whenever a problem only gives
you \bar{x}, s (or \sigma), and n rather than a raw data list.

MATH 952 skills refresher — dividing by a square root, and reading a t-table row

Standard error is a two-step calculation. SE_{\bar x} = s/\sqrt{n} means: (1) take the
square root of n first, (2) then divide s by that result — never divide first. For Example
1: \sqrt{24} \approx 4.899, then 12.24 / 4.899 \approx 2.50. Skipping straight to
“12.24/24” gives a wrong, much smaller number.

Reading a t-table. A printed t-table has one row per df and one column per confidence level
(or per tail area). Find your row (df = n-1), then the column for your confidence level, and
read off t^* — no interpolation needed for the values used in this course. The row for
df = 23 (Example 1) reads:

df

90%

95%

99%

23

1.714

2.069

2.807

Notice t^* grows as confidence grows (a wider interval to be more sure) — the same pattern
you saw with z^* back in Week 10.

A campus wellness survey plans to estimate mean daily screen time from a random sample of
n = 18 students. The sample’s histogram shows one clear peak, roughly symmetric shape, and no
outliers. Is it reasonable to use t-procedures here? Explain using both conditions from this
week (independence, and sample size/shape).

A sample of n = 36 receipts at a campus café gives \bar{x} = \$6.40 and s = \$1.80. Find
the standard error of the mean. (Do not build the full interval yet — just the standard error.)

A sample of n = 16 phone battery-life tests gives \bar{x} = 8.2 hours and s = 1.6 hours.
Construct and interpret a 90% confidence interval for the true mean battery life.

Using the t-table row for df = 23 from this week’s skills refresher, what is t^* for a
99% confidence interval? How does it compare to the 95% value used in Worked Example 1, and
why does a higher confidence level need a larger t^*?

A streaming service claims subscribers watch an average of 90 minutes per day. A random sample
of n = 20 subscribers gives \bar{x} = 97 minutes and s = 15 minutes. Test
H_0: \mu = 90 vs. H_a: \mu > 90 at \alpha = 0.05, showing the test statistic, df,
p-value, decision, and a one-sentence conclusion in context.

Explain, in your own words, why t^* is larger than z^* for the same confidence level
when n is small, and why that gap shrinks as n grows. Use the df-vs-t^* table from
this week to support your answer.

Standard error of the mean (SE_{\bar x}) — s/\sqrt{n}; how much sample means typically
vary from the true population mean.

t-distribution — a bell-shaped distribution like the Normal curve, but with heavier tails,
used for mean inference when the population SD \sigma is unknown (estimated by s).

Degrees of freedom (df) — for one-mean inference, df = n - 1; controls how heavy the
t-distribution’s tails are.

Critical value (t^*) — the t-value cutting off the confidence level’s tail area(s);
larger than the matching z^* for small df, converging to it as df grows.

Confidence interval for a mean — \bar{x} \pm t^* \cdot s/\sqrt{n}.

One-sample t-test — tests H_0: \mu = \mu_0 using t = (\bar{x} - \mu_0)/(s/\sqrt{n}) with
df = n-1.

TInterval / T-Test — the TI-83/84 menu items (under STAT ▸ TESTS) for a one-mean
confidence interval and hypothesis test.

t.test() / tsum.test() / zsum.test() — the matching R functions: t.test() from raw
data (mosaic), tsum.test() from summary statistics, and zsum.test() as the large-sample z
equivalent when \sigma is treated as known (BSDA).

Durable skill: quantitative reasoning & quantitative communication

Reporting “the average commute exceeds 20 minutes, p = 0.0083” only helps a decision-maker if
you can also say what that means in plain language and what evidence backs it up. Employers in
every field — operations, healthcare, nonprofits, city planning — need people who can run the
right test and explain the conclusion to someone who has never heard of a p-value.

Fifteen weeks ago you met a claim — “coffee drinkers live longer,” “the shelter’s most
playful cats get adopted fastest” — and learned to ask how do they know that? before you
believed it. Since then you’ve built, one week at a time, an entire toolkit for answering
that question with data instead of guessing. You classified variables and studies (Ch 1),
learned to summarize a batch of numbers or categories honestly (Ch 2), reasoned about chance
with probability and expected value (Ch 3), met the Normal curve and learned to compute exact
areas and percentiles under it (Ch 4), and then spent the second half of the semester on the
two ideas that connect the whole course: a confidence interval estimates an unknown
population value, and a hypothesis test checks whether a specific claimed value is
believable, once you account for ordinary sampling variability (Ch 5). The last two chapters
put that logic to work on the two most common real-world questions — what percent...?
(Ch 6, one proportion) and what’s the average...? (Ch 7, one mean). This week does three

The arc of the semester, in seven steps

records.content:
If you can say what each line below means and give one example of your own, you have the
whole course in your hands:

Data & study design (Ch 1) — where the numbers came from, and whether the design
supports a cause-and-effect claim.

Summarizing data (Ch 2) — turning a messy list of numbers or categories into a
handful of trustworthy numbers and honest graphs.

Probability (Ch 3, §3.1) — the rules for combining chances (complement, addition,
multiplication) and what “independent” means.

Random variables & the Normal curve (Ch 3, §3.4–3.5 → Ch 4) — expected value and
spread of a chance process, and exact areas/percentiles under a bell curve.

Sampling distributions, CIs, and testing logic (Ch 5) — why a sample statistic
wobbles from sample to sample, and the two general tools (interval, test) built on that
fact.

Inference for one proportion (Ch 6) — the tools of step 5, made concrete for a
percentage question.

Inference for one mean (Ch 7) — the same tools, made concrete for an average
question.

Every later step uses the machinery of the steps before it — nothing in this course is a
free-standing fact you memorized in isolation. That’s also why the final is comprehensive:
a one-mean test (step 7) only makes sense if you still remember what a p-value is (step 5)
and why standard deviation matters (step 2).

hierarchy.lvl2: Review checklist: Chapter 6 — Inference for One Proportion (Week 13)
Review checklist: Chapter 6 — Inference for One Proportion (Week 13)

records.content:
Recognize a one-proportion scenario: the variable of interest is categorical with
two outcomes (success/failure), and the question is about the population proportion
p having that outcome.

Check the success–failure condition before trusting the Normal-based procedure:
for a test, n p_0 \ge 10 and n(1-p_0) \ge 10 using the claimed proportion p_0;
for an interval, n\hat p \ge 10 and n(1-\hat p)\ge 10 using the sample proportion
\hat p. Also check the sample is random/independent.

Build a confidence interval: \hat p \pm z^* \cdot SE_{\hat p}, where
SE_{\hat p} = \sqrt{\hat p (1-\hat p)/n} — the standard error uses \hat p (you don’t
know p; you’re trying to estimate it).

Run a hypothesis test: state H_0: p = p_0 vs. H_A: p \ne p_0 (or <, > for a
one-sided claim); the test statistic z = (\hat p - p_0)/SE_{p_0} uses
SE_{p_0} = \sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n} — this time the standard error uses the claimed value
p_0, because the test asks “if p_0 were true, how surprising is my \hat p?”

State the decision (reject / fail to reject H_0) by comparing the p-value to \alpha,
then translate that decision into a plain-language conclusion about the original
claim, not just about H_0.

hierarchy.lvl2: Review checklist: Chapter 7 — Inference for One Mean (Week 14–15)
Review checklist: Chapter 7 — Inference for One Mean (Week 14–15)

records.content:
Recognize a one-mean scenario: the variable of interest is numerical, and the
question is about the population mean \mu.

Check conditions: the sample is random/independent, and the sample is either large
(n \ge 30 is the usual rough guideline) or shows no strong skew/outliers if smaller — you
cannot skip this check just because n “feels big enough.”

Build a confidence interval: \bar x \pm t^* \cdot SE_{\bar x}, where
SE_{\bar x} = s/\sqrt{n} and t^* comes from the t-distribution with
df = n-1 degrees of freedom (not the same z^* you used in Ch 6, though the two are
close for large n).

Run a hypothesis test: state H_0: \mu = \mu_0 vs. H_A; the test statistic is
t = (\bar x - \mu_0)/(s/\sqrt n), again with df = n-1.

Remember the reason we lead with t rather than z here: your text and your TI-84’s
native menu (TInterval/T-Test) both use t, and t automatically becomes almost
identical to z once n is large — you are not learning two different ideas, just one
idea with a slightly more honest standard curve for finite samples.

As in Ch 6: translate the reject/fail-to-reject decision into a sentence about the
original claim, in the original units (hours, dollars, minutes — never just “\mu”).

On your TI-83/84 & in R — the cross-procedure drill

Practice reaching for the right menu item / function without being told the chapter —
that’s exactly what the final will ask you to do.

Task

TI-83/84

R (mosaic/BSDA)

Normal area (probability)

2ND VARS(DISTR) ▸ normalcdf(lower,upper,μ,σ)

xpnorm(q, mean=, sd=)

Normal percentile (inverse)

invNorm(area,μ,σ)

xqnorm(p, mean=, sd=)

One-proportion interval

STAT ▸ TESTS ▸ 1-PropZInt

prop.test(x, n, conf.level=)$conf.int

One-proportion test

STAT ▸ TESTS ▸ 1-PropZTest

prop.test(x, n, p=, alternative=, correct=FALSE)

One-mean interval

STAT ▸ TESTS ▸ TInterval

tsum.test(mean.x=, s.x=, n.x=, conf.level=)$conf.int

One-mean test

STAT ▸ TESTS ▸ T-Test

tsum.test(mean.x=, s.x=, n.x=, mu=)

(In R, correct = FALSE tells prop.test() to skip the continuity correction it applies by
default, so its p-value matches the TI-84’s 1-PropZTest and the by-hand formula you learned
— worth remembering if you ever compare the two and the p-values look slightly different.)
